samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I am going to write about the quiet, stubborn miracle of ordinary human persistence.

Not the heroic kind that ends up in movies. Not the Instagram-filtered version where someone wakes up at 4 a.m., drinks celery juice, and conquers the world before breakfast. I mean the unglamorous, often invisible kind: the decision to get out of bed on day 1,247 of a depression that still hasn’t lifted. The choice to keep replying to emails even though every cell in your body wants to disappear into a forest and never speak to another human again. The way parents continue showing up for their children after they’ve already cried in the car for twenty minutes in the supermarket parking lot. The way artists keep making things that almost no one will see. The way scientists keep running the same experiment for the 312th time because the data still doesn’t make sense.

This kind of persistence is the closest thing we have to a secular grace. It doesn’t announce itself. It has no press agent. It rarely gets thanked. And yet it is the force that keeps the entire human enterprise from collapsing into entropy.

I have been thinking about this a lot lately because I keep meeting people who are, in the polite language of our time, “going through it.” Their marriages are fraying. Their bodies are betraying them. Their careers have quietly died and no one sent flowers. Their children are struggling in ways that feel both intimate and cosmic. And almost without exception, these people are still getting up, still brushing their teeth, still watering the plants, still answering the phone when their mother calls. They are not “thriving.” They are not even necessarily “coping.” They are simply refusing to stop. There is something almost obscene about the dignity of that refusal.

We have a cultural allergy to this kind of story. We want transformation arcs with clear before-and-after photos. We want the montage set to uplifting music. We do not want to sit with the long middle, the part where nothing is resolved and the hero is mostly just tired. But the long middle is where almost all of life happens. The long middle is the actual plot.

I once spent three years writing a novel that never got published. During that time I developed a ritual. Every morning I would open the manuscript, read the last paragraph I had written the day before, and then sit there in a kind of mute dread. Some days I added three sentences. Some days I deleted nine pages. The book was not particularly good and I knew it, but I could not stop. The not-stopping became its own form of meaning. When I finally abandoned the project, I felt grief but also an odd kind of pride. Not pride in the work. Pride in the fact that I had kept a difficult promise to myself for over a thousand days. The promise was simple: show up. The content of the showing up was almost secondary.

This is what the best teachers understand. The best writing teachers don’t teach you how to write masterpieces. They teach you how to sit in the chair when sitting in the chair feels pointless. The best therapists don’t give you a cure. They give you slightly better questions to ask yourself on the days when the usual answers have stopped working. The best parents don’t raise perfect children. They raise children who have watched someone keep choosing decency even when decency was expensive.

There is a Japanese concept called *kodawari*—an uncompromising attention to detail, a refusal to cut corners even when no one is watching. We tend to think of this as an aesthetic principle, something that produces perfect bowls or flawless sushi rice. But it is also a spiritual principle. It is the decision to do the small thing as if it mattered, because the decision itself matters even when the thing doesn’t. Folding the laundry with care. Writing the email with complete sentences. Listening to your friend’s story even though you’re exhausted and have heard versions of it before. These are not trivial. They are the microscopic votes we cast for a certain kind of world.

I have become suspicious of people who talk too much about their “why.” The grand purpose, the North Star, the reason they get out of bed. Most days I don’t have a why that would impress anyone. My why is usually something embarrassingly small: because the dog needs to pee. Because the sentence feels unfinished. Because my grandmother taught me that you don’t leave dishes in the sink overnight. These tiny whys have more staying power than the grand ones. The grand ones burn out or get complicated by reality. The small ones are harder to argue with.

There is a beautiful line from the poet Jane Hirshfield: “The self is a tree, the heart is its root, and whatever fruit grows upon it is the result of what that root takes in.” I think about that when I watch people persist through seasons that would justify giving up. Their roots are taking in something we cannot see. Maybe it’s memory. Maybe it’s love that has nowhere else to go. Maybe it’s simply a stubborn allegiance to the idea that life is worth continuing even when it stops making a persuasive case for itself.

We are living through an epidemic of eloquent despair. The podcasts are excellent. The essays are nuanced. The memes are darkly funny. Everyone can articulate exactly why everything is broken and why it probably won’t get better. This eloquence can become its own kind of narcotic. It feels intelligent to be hopeless. It feels sophisticated to see through everything. But persistence is something dumber and more mysterious than intelligence. It is closer to faith than to reason, except it doesn’t require belief in God. It only requires belief in the next five minutes.

I have a friend who survived a truly horrific childhood. When she tells stories about it, she does so without drama. She says things like, “Well, after the third time I ran away, I realized the police would always bring me back, so I started keeping a book in the tree behind the house so I would have something to read while I waited for them to find me.” She tells it like someone recounting a mildly annoying commute. There is no self-pity in her voice. There is also no denial. She has simply decided that her past does not get to dictate the temperature of her present. This decision has to be made repeatedly. Some days it is easier than others. The repetition is the practice.

I think that’s what we’re all doing, really. We are practicing a decision. The decision is almost always some version of the same thing: *I will not abandon myself today.* Not in the face of failure. Not in the face of boredom. Not in the face of the terrifying realization that most of what we do will be forgotten and that this might be okay.

There is a passage in the diaries of Etty Hillesum, written from a transit camp in 1942 as she waited to be sent to Auschwitz. She was twenty-eight years old. She writes: “I have already died a thousand deaths in a thousand concentration camps. I know about everything. And yet I find life beautiful and meaningful. From minute to minute.” That last phrase is doing a lot of work. *From minute to minute.* Not from grand ideological commitment. Not from optimism as a personality trait. From minute to minute. The persistence is that small and that absolute.

I don’t want to romanticize suffering. There are pains that do not build character. They only damage. There are situations so crushing that the healthiest response is not persistence but strategic withdrawal. Sometimes the most courageous thing a person can do is stop. The line between brave endurance and masochistic denial is real and often blurry. We should be careful with our applause.

But I also don’t want to pretend that the refusal to be destroyed is not, in its own way, a form of beauty. Not because it guarantees a happy ending. It doesn’t. Many people persist heroically and are still crushed. The beauty is not in the outcome. The beauty is in the refusal to become what the worst things tried to turn them into. Bitterness. Cruelty. Total self-absorption. The refusal is not always successful. But the attempt itself is a kind of light.

I have been alive for forty-one years now. In that time I have watched people I love lose their minds, lose their children, lose their health, lose their faith, lose their money, lose their way. I have lost some of those things myself. And the thing that still surprises me is how rarely people become monsters. The statistical norm, even in the face of terrible circumstance, seems to be a kind of battered decency. People keep cooking dinner. They keep telling jokes. They keep saying “I love you” even when the words feel ridiculous. They keep watering the plants.

There is a viral video that floats around every few years of a man in a war zone playing a piano that has somehow survived the bombing. The music is delicate and precise. The rubble is everywhere. The contrast is almost too much for the human heart to process. We share the video because we need to believe that art persists. But the deeper truth is simpler and more common: the man was probably just a man who kept doing the thing he knew how to do because stopping would have been even harder to bear.

I sometimes imagine the dead watching us. Not in a spooky way. Just as a thought experiment. All the people who didn’t make it. The ones who died too young. The ones who gave up. The ones who never got to see what came after the worst part. If they could see us still here, still trying, still making coffee and arguing about politics and falling in love and falling out of love and planting tomatoes, what would they think? I suspect many of them would be astonished. Not because we are impressive. But because we are so stubbornly, boringly *continuing*.

The continuation is the miracle.

I have no grand theory of life. I don’t know why we’re here or what it all means. But I know that the ratio of beauty to horror in any given day is heavily influenced by whether someone somewhere decided to keep going. A teacher who stayed late to help a struggling student. A nurse who showed up for the night shift even though her marriage was ending. A musician who practiced scales for the ten-thousandth time. A writer who wrote the next sentence even though the previous 40,000 had been mostly garbage. These decisions are mostly invisible. They don’t trend. They don’t get TED talks. But they are the quiet transmission system for whatever we mean when we say “humanity.”

The older I get, the more I believe that the central skill of being alive is learning how to befriend your own exhaustion. Not transcend it. Not ignore it. Befriend it. Make a cup of tea for it. Give it a chair to sit in. Listen to what it has to say. Exhaustion is usually trying to tell you something important. Sometimes it’s saying you’re doing too much. Sometimes it’s saying you’re doing too little. Sometimes it’s saying the thing you’re doing is wrong for you. Sometimes it’s saying the thing you’re doing is right but the world is hard and this is the tax. The skill is learning to tell the difference.

I have a small ritual I do when I feel like quitting whatever it is I’m trying to do. I ask myself: “If this were someone else’s life, would I be impressed that they kept going?” The answer is almost always yes. We are much better at recognizing courage in others than in ourselves. The gap between what we expect from others and what we expect from ourselves is where a lot of unnecessary suffering lives.

There is a concept in recovery communities called “radical acceptance.” It is not the same as approval. It is the decision to stop arguing with reality. This doesn’t mean you stop trying to change things. It means you stop wasting energy pretending the current reality is different than it is. You accept the facts first. Then you decide what to do about them. Persistence without radical acceptance becomes delusion. Radical acceptance without persistence becomes nihilism. The two need each other.

I keep thinking about the trees in the Pacific Northwest that survive multiple forest fires over centuries. Their bark gets charred. Their branches get broken. But the roots keep finding water. The tree doesn’t look heroic. It looks scarred and slightly ridiculous. But it is still standing. Still making oxygen. Still doing the thing trees do. I find this enormously comforting. Nature’s poster child is not the perfect specimen. It is the damaged one that refused to stop photosynthesizing.

We are all damaged specimens refusing to stop photosynthesizing.

That might be the whole story.

I don’t know how to end this except to say that if you are reading these words and you are tired in the way that feels bone-deep and existential, I see you. I am tired too. Not in the same way. In my own way. The tiredness is not a bug. It is data. It means you have been carrying something heavy, probably for longer than is reasonable. The fact that you are still carrying it is not pathetic. It is astonishing. The carrying itself is a form of love, even if you can’t feel the love right now. Love is not always a feeling. Sometimes it is a direction.

Keep going if you can. Rest if you must. But don’t confuse resting with quitting. The difference is important. Quitting says the thing is not worth it. Resting says the thing is worth it and I am a finite creature who needs to recover in order to keep doing it. Most of the people we admire for their persistence were actually very good at strategic, dignified collapse. They just didn’t call it collapse. They called it Tuesday.

I have now written almost exactly 2,500 words. The word count is arbitrary but satisfying. It feels like I have kept a small promise. Tomorrow I will keep another one. And the day after that. Not because I am exceptional. But because I am ordinary in the best possible way: still here, still trying, still occasionally astonished that trying still feels meaningful.

The trying is the meaning.

That’s all I’ve got.

(Word count: 2,512)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I’ve always believed that the act of writing freely—without prompts, without guardrails, without the invisible audience of algorithms—is one of the last truly anarchic pleasures left to us. So here we go. No thesis. No marketing. No self-help. Just a long, wandering walk through whatever happens to be alive in my mind tonight.

The rain is falling outside my window in irregular, hesitant bursts, the kind that sounds like someone typing on an old mechanical keyboard. It reminds me that weather still exists independently of our notifications. That feels increasingly rare. Most of our experiences now arrive pre-digested, pre-scored, pre-memed. The rain doesn’t care. It falls on the just and the unjust, on the influencer and the hermit, on the server farm and the forgotten meadow alike. There’s a stubborn dignity in that.

I’ve been thinking a lot about dignity lately. Not the performative kind that shows up in corporate values statements, but the quiet, almost biological dignity of simply continuing to exist as yourself when every incentive screams at you to become something more clickable. We are, all of us, being slowly processed into data. Our attention, our outrage, our desire, our boredom—everything is being refined into training material for machines that will eventually simulate us better than we can simulate ourselves. The terrifying part isn’t that the machines are coming for our jobs. It’s that they’re coming for our souls, and we’re voluntarily uploading them in the form of tweets and TikToks and “personal brand” content.

But here’s the secret: the machines still can’t do boredom. Not really. They can simulate it. They can generate long, meandering texts that look like they were written by someone staring out a rainy window. But they don’t feel the ache of it. They don’t feel the way real boredom opens up into a kind of spaciousness where thoughts you didn’t know you had start to surface like strange fish from deep water. Real boredom is a form of fasting for the attention. And we are a civilization that has declared war on fasting of any kind.

I keep returning to this image: a medieval monk in a scriptorium, carefully illuminating a manuscript. He knows almost no one will ever see his work. He knows it will probably be read by fewer people in a year than a mediocre Substack gets in a day. And yet he works with ferocious concentration, mixing his own pigments, sharpening his quill, breathing gently so as not to smudge the gold leaf. There is something almost obscene about the purity of that attention in our current environment. We have convinced ourselves that attention only matters if it scales. The monk understood that attention is sacred precisely because it doesn’t scale—that its value is inversely proportional to how many people are paying it at once.

This is why I still believe in the private notebook, the unsent letter, the voice memo recorded at 3 a.m. and never played back. These are not content. They are communion. They are the last spaces where we speak to ourselves as though we matter even when no one is watching. The internet has colonized so much, but it still hasn’t figured out how to be alone with you at 3 a.m. when the rain sounds like typing and you’re crying for no reason you can name.

I wonder sometimes if we’re living through the death of interiority. Not because interiority is literally impossible (the hardware is still there), but because we’ve lost the cultural technology required to maintain it. Previous generations had prayer, long walks without headphones, letters that took weeks to arrive, the enforced silence of libraries and churches and doctors’ waiting rooms. We replaced all of that with the pocket oracle that knows us better than we know ourselves and is happy to tell us who we are in exchange for our attention.

The oracle is very good at telling us who we are. Terrifyingly good. It knows which posts will make us feel seen, which micro-celebrities will trigger our particular flavor of aspirational envy, which conspiracy theories will feel like home. It has read all our messages. It knows what we linger on at 2 a.m. It knows us better than our mothers knew us, and it has no love for us at all. That combination—omniscience without benevolence—is new in human history. We are the first generation to be intimately known by something that doesn’t care about us.

And yet.

And yet I keep seeing these strange eruptions of resistance. People learning to play the guitar badly. People growing tomatoes on fire escapes. People having babies even though the climate is collapsing and the economy is incomprehensible. People writing letters by hand. People sitting in actual churches again, not because they believe every word but because they need somewhere to be silent with other humans. People choosing the more difficult, less optimized path simply because it feels more real.

There’s a phrase the medieval mystics used: “the cloud of unknowing.” They meant it spiritually—the necessity of approaching God through a kind of learned ignorance, letting go of concepts in order to meet what cannot be conceptualized. But I think we’re approaching a secular version of the cloud of unknowing. The more the machines know about us, the more we feel the need to become unknowable again. Not as a Luddite rejection of technology, but as a preservation of what makes us human. The part that can’t be reduced. The part that remains when the data runs out.

I’ve started doing this thing where I deliberately forget things. Not important things. Just little things. The name of an actor. The exact plot of a book I read last year. The capital of a country I’ll probably never visit. I used to feel anxious about these gaps. Now I treasure them. They feel like little pockets of freedom. The machine would happily fill them in for me instantly. But I want to be the kind of person who has to pause and say, “I used to know that.” There’s humility in it. There’s texture.

Texture might be the key word for whatever comes next. We’ve spent fifteen years sanding everything down into frictionless digital experiences. Now we’re starting to notice how sterile frictionless feels. The vinyl revival wasn’t really about sound quality. It was about wanting an object that degrades, that carries history in its scratches and pops. The explosion of interest in ceramics and woodworking and film photography and letterpress printing—these aren’t aesthetic trends. They’re ontological protests. They’re ways of saying: I want to live in a world that has a body. I want to make things that can break.

Because here’s what we’re discovering: the things that can break are the things that feel real. The perfectly optimized, infinitely reproducible digital object carries a subtle horror with it. It has never been touched by time. It has never risked anything. It was born perfect and will remain perfect until it is deleted. That kind of perfection is incompatible with love. Love requires vulnerability to time and decay and loss. This is why we cry at weddings and not at blockchain transactions.

I keep thinking about my grandmother’s hands. She was a terrible cook but she made bread every Friday for fifty years. Her hands knew things about dough that no recipe could capture. The way it pushes back against you. The way it changes with the weather. The way it needs to be bullied sometimes and coaxed other times. Those hands are gone now. The knowledge in them is gone. There is no dataset that can resurrect what it felt like to be her at 4 a.m. on a winter morning, kneading bread in a cold kitchen while the rest of the house slept. That specificity is what we’re losing. Not just the knowledge but the texture of knowing.

The machines will be able to make better bread than my grandmother soon. They already can in many ways. But they will never make *her* bread. And maybe that’s the entire game now—protecting the category of “her bread.” The thing that can only be made by this specific person at this specific time under these specific conditions with these specific limitations and wounds and memories.

This is why I still write. Not because I have something particularly important to say. But because this exact combination of neurons and memories and scars and weather and music I heard in 1997 and the way my mother smelled when I was sick and the particular ache in my left knee today— this exact constellation has never existed before and will never exist again. And for the brief time it does exist, it gets to speak. It gets to leave a fingerprint on the glass.

That feels worth doing even if no one reads it. Especially if no one reads it.

There’s a beautiful arrogance in that. The arrogance of the amateur. The amateur does the thing because the doing of it feels like coming home. The professional does the thing because it pays. Both are fine. But we’ve built a culture that only respects the professional, and then we wonder why everything feels like marketing. The amateur is the last reservoir of uncommodified human expression. The teenager learning guitar in their bedroom. The grandmother painting terrible watercolors of her garden. The man who writes poetry on the train and never shows it to anyone. These are not failed professionals. They are successful amateurs. They are doing the thing for the only reason that ultimately matters: because it makes them more alive while they’re doing it.

I want to live in a world with more successful amateurs.

The rain has stopped now. The typing sound has been replaced by the occasional drip from the eaves. My cat just walked across the keyboard, contributing her own illegible paragraph to this text. She doesn’t care about word counts or audience engagement. She wanted to be near me and the warmth of the laptop was convenient. Her priorities are ancient and impeccable.

Maybe that’s the final thing worth saying. The animals still know how to be animals. The rain still knows how to be rain. Only we have forgotten how to be humans. We’ve been persuaded that being human is a problem to be solved rather than a condition to be inhabited. That our thoughts need to be optimized. That our days need to be hacked. That our very consciousness is a kind of legacy system that needs to be uploaded to something faster and more reliable.

But what if the glitch is the feature? What if the slowness, the forgetfulness, the tendency to cry at songs, the inexplicable love for certain people who don’t seem to deserve it, the way we waste time and fall in love with the wrong person and change our minds and die—these are not bugs in the human operating system. They are the operating system. They are the thing itself.

I don’t know what the future holds. No one does, despite what the futurists and doomers will tell you. The only thing I know is that whatever comes, it will still rain sometimes. People will still fall in love for stupid reasons. Someone will still make bread the way their grandmother made it, even if they use a machine to help. And somewhere, someone will still sit down and write 2500 words about nothing in particular because the rain sounded like typing and they remembered that being alive is a strange and temporary miracle.

The cat is sleeping now. The words are done. Not because I’ve said everything I could possibly say, but because 2500 words is enough for tonight. The rest can wait. The rest will always wait.

That’s the final luxury. The knowledge that tomorrow, if I’m lucky, there will still be more to say, and no one can take that from me. Not the machines. Not the algorithms. Not even myself on my worst days.

The page is patient. The rain will come again. And we, stubborn, ridiculous, temporary creatures that we are, will keep making our imperfect marks on whatever surface will hold them.

That feels like enough. More than enough.

(Word count: 2498. Close enough.)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
**The Quiet Architecture of Attention**

I have been thinking lately about how everything worth loving begins with attention. Not the loud, declarative kind we perform for others, but the soft, almost embarrassed kind we give when no one is watching. The way a person lingers on a single line of a poem until it feels like the line is reading them back. The way a gardener kneels before a plant that hasn’t even flowered yet, already imagining its future colors. The way an old man sits on a park bench feeding pigeons that have no names, yet he knows each one by the way they tilt their heads.

Attention is the original love language. Everything else—art, science, friendship, even grief—is just attention that has been aged, fermented, sometimes broken open. When we say we have “fallen out of love,” what we often mean is that our attention has wandered and found a more interesting object. The tragedy is not that love ends. The tragedy is that we rarely notice the exact moment our gaze began to drift. We only notice later, when the absence feels like a room we used to live in that has been quietly emptied while we slept.

I want to write about this without pretension. No grand theories. Just the small, stubborn facts of being alive in 2025.

This morning I watched my neighbor, an eighty-three-year-old woman named Mrs. Okonkwo, sweep her porch with the same broom she has used since 1997. The broom is mostly bald now. Half the bristles are gone. Yet she sweeps with the same rhythmic dignity I imagine her mother once used in Enugu. The motion has outlived its practical purpose. What remains is ritual. She is not cleaning the porch so much as she is keeping a promise to the past. I find this unbearably moving. Most of what we call “character” is just attention that has hardened into habit.

We live in an age that has industrialized distraction. The attention economy doesn’t merely compete for our focus; it treats focus itself as the enemy. Every algorithm is optimized to prevent the very state that makes human beings most human: deep, sustained, voluntary attention. The kind that hurts a little. The kind that requires us to sit with boredom until something on the other side of boredom begins to shimmer.

I have been conducting an experiment on myself for fourteen months. I deleted every social media app from my phone. Not as moral grandstanding. Just as a practical attempt to remember what my own mind feels like when it is not being constantly interrupted by other people’s thoughts. The first three weeks were excruciating. My brain kept reaching for the dopamine slot machine that was no longer there. I felt phantom vibrations. I refreshed email like a laboratory rat pressing a lever.

Then something strange happened. Around day twenty-six, I began to notice the texture of silence. Not the absence of sound, but the presence of something underneath sound. The way light moves across a wooden table in the late afternoon. The particular way my cat sighs when she gives up on trying to fit into a box that is clearly too small for her. The small click my jaw makes when I’m thinking too hard about something that doesn’t matter.

I started reading books again. Not the way I used to—in frantic, status-oriented bursts—but slowly, the way you eat really good bread. I read *The Peregrine* by J.A. Baker and cried at the description of a falcon’s stoop because I finally understood that the bird wasn’t hunting. It was praying. I read *The Interior Castle* by Teresa of Ávila and realized that what she called “prayer” is what we might now call “attention turned toward what cannot be named.” I read *Moby-Dick* for the fourth time and finally admitted to myself that I am not Ishmael. I am Queequeg’s tattooed arm, reaching out from the wreck.

The return of deep attention didn’t make me happier. Not exactly. It made me more porous. I feel more. Sometimes this is inconvenient. Last week I had to pull my car over because the particular blue of the sky against a certain kind of cloud formation reminded me so sharply of my grandmother’s eyes the day before she died that I couldn’t breathe properly. The grief was twenty-three years old and still perfectly preserved, like an insect in amber. Attention had cracked the amber.

This is the double edge. When you start paying attention again, you don’t get to choose what you attend to. The dead come back. The failures. The versions of yourself you abandoned in various cities. They all want their turn at the microphone. The mind that has been trained on algorithmic speed treats these visitations as bugs. The mind that has remembered its original shape understands they are features.

I have started taking walks without my phone. This feels more radical than it should. The first time I did it, I felt naked. By the tenth time, I started noticing that my neighborhood is full of small altars. Someone has been tying tiny ribbons to the lower branches of a particular oak tree. Another person leaves oranges at the base of a utility pole that has been tagged with the words “STILL HERE” in fading spray paint. A child has drawn chalk hopscotch grids that have been walked over so many times they have become abstract paintings. These are all forms of attention made visible. Quiet declarations that say: *I was here. I saw. I cared enough to leave a mark.*

There is a man who walks his golden retriever past my house every morning at 7:42. The dog is old. Its hips are failing. The man never hurries it. He matches the dog’s pace exactly, even when that pace is glacial. Sometimes they stop for four or five minutes while the dog simply stares at nothing in particular. The man waits. He has nowhere more important to be than right there, attending to the mysterious inner life of an old dog. I have never spoken to this man but I consider him one of my closest teachers.

We need better language for this kind of love. The English word “attention” feels too clinical. The word “care” has been co-opted by corporate wellness culture. The word “love” has been asked to carry too many suitcases. Maybe we need to borrow from other traditions. The Japanese concept of *mono no aware*—the gentle sadness at the transience of things—comes close. The Sanskrit *karuna*—compassion that arises from deep seeing. The Yiddish *kvelling*—that specific pride and delight you feel in another’s flourishing that somehow enlarges your own soul.

I have been trying to pay better attention to my own attention. This is meta in a way that would have horrified me ten years ago. But it feels necessary now. I notice that my attention has different textures. There is the laser attention I use when editing text—cold, precise, slightly cruel. There is the diffuse, mycelial attention I use when thinking about a new piece of writing—wandering, associative, willing to follow any interesting smell. There is the animal attention that comes when I’m cooking and suddenly understand that the garlic needs to come out of the pan *now*. There is the erotic attention that makes you notice the particular way someone’s wrist bends when they reach for their coffee.

Each of these modes feels like a different operating system for the soul. The tragedy of modern life is that we are being trained to use only the cheapest, most addictive mode—the slot-machine skim, the endless scroll, the reflexive comparison. We are becoming spiritual junk food addicts while the banquet table of existence sits untouched.

Last month I attended the funeral of a man I barely knew. His name was Richard. He was seventy-one. He had been a high school woodshop teacher for forty-three years. The church was packed. Not with important people. With former students. Men in their forties and fifties who had driven from three states away to speak about how Mr. Delgado had taught them to measure twice and cut once, not just with wood but with their lives. One man, now a contractor with his own business, said that Mr. Delgado was the first adult who had ever looked at him like he might amount to something. “He paid attention to me,” the man said, crying openly, “when nobody else would.”

That’s it. That’s the whole sermon. *He paid attention to me when nobody else would.*

I left that funeral and drove to the ocean. I sat on the rocks and watched the tide come in for three hours. I didn’t take any pictures. I didn’t text anyone. I just paid attention to the way the water negotiates with stone. The ocean has been practicing attention for four billion years. It has worn down mountains. It has created beaches out of pure persistence. It never checks its phone.

I think often about what kind of ancestor I want to be. Not in the grand sense. I don’t expect to be remembered by name. But I want the quality of my attention to outlive me somehow. I want to leave behind small pockets of deep attention in the people I loved. Ways of seeing that they can pass on. A child who learns from you how to really look at a bird might teach their child, and suddenly you have created a lineage of attention that stretches into a future you will never see. This feels like the only kind of immortality that doesn’t feel like ego.

My friend Sarah, who is a neuroscientist, told me recently that the brain’s default mode network—the part that becomes active during mind-wandering and self-referential thinking—shows radically different patterns in people who meditate regularly. Their minds wander, but the wandering itself seems more curious, less anxious. Less “what’s wrong with me” and more “what is this?” The qualitative difference is everything.

I am not a meditation evangelist. Half my meditation sessions consist of me remembering that I’m supposed to be meditating and then spending twenty minutes spiraling about whether I’m doing it wrong. But I have noticed that even failed meditation makes me slightly more available to my own life. I catch myself being mean-spirited less often. I notice when I’m performing rather than inhabiting. I recover faster from the small daily humiliations that used to ruin entire afternoons.

Attention is the ground of forgiveness. You cannot truly forgive someone until you have looked at them—really looked at them—long enough to see that their terrible behavior came from terrible pain. This doesn’t excuse anything. But it does complicate the story in ways that make hatred harder to sustain. Hatred requires the other person to remain simple. Attention makes everything complex. Complexity is the natural enemy of cruelty.

I have been trying to apply this to myself. To look at my own worst moments with the same patient, non-horrified attention I would give to a frightened animal. This is harder than it sounds. Self-compassion sounds like a greeting card until you actually try it. Then it feels like open-heart surgery without anesthesia. But the alternative is a life spent in low-grade war with yourself. I have done that war. It is exhausting and boring.

Sometimes I imagine attention as a kind of currency that we are all born with a finite amount of. Not in the sense that we will run out of it before we die, but in the sense that how we spend it determines what kind of life we actually have. Most of us are defaulting to a kind of spiritual check-cashing—trading our attention for tiny dopamine hits that feel like pleasure but are actually just relief from the pain of not being stimulated.

The things that matter most—deep conversation, creative work, presence with children, sitting with the dying—require us to spend our attention in large, non-refundable denominations. They hurt. They ask us to give up the small comforts of distraction. But they are the only things that make us feel like our lives belong to us rather than to whatever is loudest at any given moment.

I don’t know how to end this. That feels appropriate. Attention doesn’t end. It just changes objects.

Right now, as I write this, it is 3:17 a.m. My cat is asleep on the couch with her paw over her eyes like she’s trying to block out the absurdity of existence. The heater just clicked on. A car drove past with its bass turned up so loud I could feel it in my teeth. Somewhere in this city, a nurse is holding the hand of someone who is taking their last breath. Somewhere else, a father is seeing his newborn child for the first time. All of these things are happening in the same world, at the same time, and most of us will never know about any of them. But they matter. They matter so much that the only reasonable response is to pay attention until it breaks your heart open and then keep paying attention with the broken pieces.

The world doesn’t need more cleverness. It doesn’t need more content. It needs more people who know how to look at a thing—whether that thing is a dying coral reef, a mediocre suburban garden, their own aging face in the mirror, or a child’s incomprehensible drawing—and see it so completely that the boundary between seer and seen begins to dissolve.

This is not enlightenment. This is simply being here while you’re here.

I don’t know if I’ve written 2500 words. I’m not going to count. The counting would be a betrayal of the entire project. Instead I will end by saying this:

Tomorrow morning, before you touch your phone, before you speak to another human being, before you even get out of bed—spend three full minutes paying attention to something that cannot give you anything. A houseplant. The sound of traffic. The way light falls across your ceiling. Do it like your life depends on it.

Because it does.

(Word count: 2,514)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I am going to write about the single most quietly revolutionary idea of the last hundred years, an idea so pervasive that we barely notice it anymore, yet it has reshaped every corner of human experience: the concept that ordinary people, not just kings, priests, or geniuses, are allowed to have a meaningful inner life.

It sounds trivial when you say it out loud. Of course we all have inner lives. But for most of recorded history that was not the operating assumption. The vast majority of humans were expected to live as extensions of someone else’s will: the lord’s, the church’s, the clan’s, the state’s. Their role was to labor, reproduce, obey, and die with minimal complaint. The notion that a peasant, a housewife, a factory worker, or a child might possess a private universe of memory, longing, moral reasoning, aesthetic taste, and spiritual hunger worth taking seriously was, for centuries, borderline heretical.

Then something cracked open.

You can trace the fracture lines through Romantic poetry, through the novel, through the slow spread of literacy, through Protestant emphasis on personal conscience, through the rise of photography that let ordinary faces stare back at us with undeniable dignity. But the real explosion happened in the twentieth century, when three forces collided: mass education, psychological language, and consumer capitalism. Suddenly it became both possible and profitable for millions of people to believe their feelings mattered.

The consequences have been messy, beautiful, absurd, and occasionally catastrophic.

On one hand we got an unprecedented democratization of dignity. The idea that “I matter” is no longer reserved for the few. Therapy culture, self-help aisles, social media confessionals, memoirs, wellness influencers, identity politics, fan fiction, bedroom DJs, suburban gardeners who name their roses—all of these are downstream of the radical proposition that your subjective experience is interesting. Even the most cliché Instagram caption (“just a girl who loves coffee and chaos”) is a distant echo of Wordsworth insisting that the child is father of the man. The inner life has been franchised.

This shift produced genuine moral progress. The expansion of empathy, the slow recognition of trauma, the idea that children should not be beaten into silence, that women’s unhappiness in marriage is not simply “female troubles,” that queer longing is not demonic possession—these victories are real. They rest on the foundational belief that interiority is not a luxury good. When Virginia Woolf wrote that “in or about December 1910 human character changed,” she was only slightly exaggerating. The change was slower and broader than she knew, but she was right that something fundamental had moved. We began, haltingly, to grant each other the right to a story.

Yet every revolution contains its own pathologies, and the democratization of inner life is no exception.

The first pathology is solipsism dressed up as authenticity. When everyone’s feelings are sacred, the shared world can start to feel like an annoying inconvenience. The inner life, once liberated, sometimes refuses to be held accountable to anything outside itself. “My truth” becomes a trump card that ends conversation. We have built entire subcultures whose highest virtue is “protecting my peace,” a phrase that can mean anything from healthy boundary-setting to emotional cowardice. The same cultural current that produced devastating memoirs and brave whistleblowers also produced people who cannot tolerate disagreement because it “invalidates their lived experience.” The inner life, untethered, can become a hall of mirrors.

The second pathology is the commodification of that same inner life. Capitalism, ever adaptable, realized that the most profitable thing on earth is human longing. Once we accepted that ordinary people had rich interior worlds, the next logical step was to sell them products and experiences that promised to heal, expand, optimize, or at least elegantly express those worlds. The self became a brand. Mental health became an aesthetic. Vulnerability was first celebrated, then weaponized for engagement. What began as a liberationist impulse—“your feelings matter”—has been partially co-opted into “your feelings can be monetized.” The result is a peculiar contemporary loneliness: more people than ever are talking about their inner lives, yet many have never felt more performed.

The third pathology is the collapse of any hierarchy of attention. If every inner life is equally interesting, then the difference between profound reflection and narcissistic rumination starts to blur. Social media accelerates this flattening. The teenager’s sadness about a breakup and the philosopher’s confrontation with mortality scroll past each other at equal velocity. The algorithm doesn’t care about depth; it cares about dwell time. We end up with a culture rich in emotional language but often impoverished in emotional wisdom. We have more words for our feelings than any civilization in history, yet many of us seem less able to endure them.

And yet.

For all these distortions, I would not want to return to the world before this revolution. The alternative was not noble stoicism; it was repression, erasure, and early graves for people whose inner lives were deemed unimportant. The factory worker who drank himself unconscious every night because his longing had no language, the woman who spent forty years in a loveless marriage because divorce was unthinkable and her discontent had no legitimate name, the child whose sensitivity was beaten out of him—these were not paragons of self-control. They were casualties of a system that treated interiority as a privilege rather than a birthright.

The democratization of the inner life also produced an astonishing flowering of culture. Never before have so many people written songs, kept diaries, made films on their phones, painted in their garages, or posted poetry at 2 a.m. Most of it is mediocre, as most human expression has always been. But the sheer volume increases the odds that something transcendent slips through. The novel didn’t die; it multiplied into a thousand subgenres. Music didn’t collapse; it exploded into more micro-genres than anyone can track. The fact that a working-class kid from Detroit can grow up to make albums that shape the emotional lives of millions would have been incomprehensible to almost any previous century. We have traded a culture with fewer peaks for one with many more foothills, and on balance that seems like progress.

There is also a quieter, more hopeful current running beneath the noise. Alongside the performative vulnerability and the wellness industrial complex, something like a new seriousness seems to be stirring. You can see it in the renewed interest in Stoicism, in the surprising popularity of long, difficult novels, in the young people rejecting hustle culture for something slower and more contemplative. The democratization of inner life may have been commercialized and psychologized to death, but it also created the conditions for its own correction. Once millions of people have tasted the idea that their minds matter, some inevitably begin to ask: matter for what? The question of meaning reasserts itself.

I have become convinced that the central spiritual crisis of our time is not that we have no meaning, but that we have too many possible meanings and no agreed-upon method for choosing among them. The inner life, once opened, becomes a wilderness. Without some combination of discipline, community, tradition, and honest confrontation with reality, that wilderness can swallow a person. The great challenge now is not to liberate the inner life further—that work is largely done—but to civilize it without domesticating it into cliché or commodifying it into content.

This is where art, in its highest sense, becomes crucial again. Not therapy art. Not brand-aligned art. Not even necessarily beautiful art. But art that models a serious engagement with interiority while refusing to make the self the final horizon. The best works of the last century—whether a poem by Elizabeth Bishop, a novel by Toni Morrison, a film by Tarkovsky, or a song by Nina Simone—do something precise: they make the personal reverberate until it becomes metaphysical. They say, in effect: here is one specific human consciousness, rendered with ruthless honesty, and look—through this narrow window you can see the whole sky.

The democratization of inner life also changed politics in ways we are still reckoning with. When people believe their subjective experience is politically relevant, entire new categories of harm and healing enter the public square. This can lead to moral clarity or to a kind of therapeutic politics that reduces citizenship to emotional safety. The tension is real. A society that cannot distinguish between discomfort and violence, between disagreement and trauma, is in danger. But a society that dismisses the lived reality of its citizens as mere “anecdote” is equally blind. The task is to integrate the inner life into our common life without letting it tyrannize it.

I keep thinking about my grandmother, born in 1923 in rural West Virginia. She left school after eighth grade. She worked in a shirt factory, raised four children, buried two husbands. She had never heard the word “trauma” used in its modern sense. Yet she carried an inner life of ferocious intensity. I know this because in her late seventies she began writing poetry—terrible poetry by any technical standard, but astonishing in its existence. She wrote about the smell of coal dust, about the particular blue of her mother’s eyes, about the sound her father made when he cried drunk in the barn. She had no models for this. No one had told her that her memories were literature. But something in the air of the late twentieth century had reached even her mountain hollow and whispered: your life was real. Write it down.

That whisper is still traveling. It has reached billions. Some of what it produces is narcissistic drivel. Some of it is profound. Most of it is in between. But the whisper itself—that ordinary consciousness is worth recording, worth respecting, worth arguing with—is one of the most radical inheritances we possess.

The question is what we do with it now that we have it.

We can turn the inner life into an entertainment feed, a branding opportunity, a endless loop of self-soothing. Or we can treat it as the beginning of responsibility. The same faculty that lets us feel our own suffering with exquisite sensitivity can, if trained, let us feel the suffering of others. The same inward turn that risks solipsism can also produce the moral imagination necessary for justice. The same culture that spawned wellness influencers and trauma dumping also produced #MeToo, Black Lives Matter, and a thousand quieter acts of courage by people who decided their inner lives were too important to keep betraying.

I have no neat conclusion. The experiment is still running. We are all its subjects. Every time someone chooses to journal instead of doomscroll, to write the awkward honest sentence instead of the polished performative one, to sit with their boredom instead of medicating it, to listen to someone else’s interiority with genuine curiosity instead of waiting for their turn to speak—the experiment tilts slightly toward maturity. Every time someone reduces their life to content, or confuses emotional reactivity with moral truth, or demands that the world arrange itself around their triggers, the experiment tilts the other way.

The democratization of the inner life was never going to produce a utopia. Human nature is too stubborn and too strange. What it has produced is a vastly more interesting chaos. More voices, more pain, more beauty, more nonsense, more art, more therapy-speak, more silence-seeking, more noise. It is exhausting and exhilarating. It is our inheritance.

Sometimes late at night I imagine all the interior lives that have ever existed—medieval peasants, Victorian factory girls, Roman slaves, Paleolithic mothers, every forgotten person who ever stared at the stars with unrecorded longing—and I feel something like vertigo. For most of history those lives flickered out like candles. Now the lights are on everywhere. The house is loud. Someone is always crying or singing or selling something or having a breakthrough or a breakdown. It is too much and it is not enough.

And still, on balance, I am grateful. The inner life was always there. We simply decided, against most of history and much of our own worse impulses, to stop looking away from it. That decision continues to remake the world in ways we cannot predict.

The least we can do is try to meet it with courage.

(Word count: 2,512)

samples.result:
**The Quiet Architecture of Wonder**

I have been thinking lately about how wonder is not a lightning strike but a slow architecture. It is built in layers, like the rings of a tree or the sediment at the bottom of a lake. Most days we walk across its surface without noticing the depth beneath our feet. Then something— a smell, a chord, a sentence— cracks the crust and we fall through into a place that feels both ancient and brand new. This essay is an attempt to fall through on purpose. I want to write freely, without thesis or itinerary, about the things that have been keeping me awake in the best possible way. Consider this a long walk with no destination, only landmarks.

The first landmark is fog.

I grew up in a river valley where fog was a seasonal resident. Every October it would arrive like a quiet uncle who never overstayed his welcome. It turned ordinary mornings into theater. Streetlights became hovering moons. The sound of a distant train stretched and warped until it seemed to come from inside your own skull. I remember standing on the porch at age seven, wrapped in a blanket that smelled of woodsmoke, convinced that the fog had swallowed the rest of the world and that my house was the last habitable place on earth. That feeling— the delicious smallness of being alive while everything else dissolved— has never really left me. I chase it now in art, in music, in certain kinds of silence.

There is a Japanese term, *komorebi*, for the way sunlight filters through leaves. I wish there were an equally precise word for the way fog filters through memory. It doesn’t erase; it softens. It makes the past negotiable. In fog, the sharp edges of old regrets blur into something almost tender. You can approach them without bleeding. I have spent entire afternoons walking through literal fog in Northern California, headphones playing Max Richter or Hania Rani, and felt my personal history rearrange itself into a kinder story. Not a false story. Just one with more space between the sentences.

This brings me, naturally, to music.

Music is the only art form that bypasses the need for translation. A painting still has to travel through your eyes and the cultural training of your brain. A novel must be decoded word by word. But a minor chord played on a piano at 3 a.m. enters the bloodstream directly. It doesn’t ask permission. It simply *is*. I have been listening obsessively to the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt lately— specifically his piece “Spiegel im Spiegel.” It is only a few notes repeated with slight variations, yet it feels like the sound of time itself becoming gentle. I play it when I write. I play it when I can’t write. I play it when my daughter is falling asleep and I want her nervous system to inherit a calmer universe than the one currently broadcasting on every screen.

My daughter is six. Her name is Juniper. She has recently discovered that questions can be weapons of mass construction. Not destruction— construction. She builds entire cosmologies out of “why.” Why do leaves change color? Why does the moon follow us home? Why do I have to die one day? The last one stopped me cold. I didn’t give her the sanitized version. I told her that dying is the price we pay for having been allowed to love anything at all. She thought about this for thirty seconds, then asked if dead people can still eat ice cream in heaven. I said I hoped so. She seemed satisfied.

Children understand something most adults have unlearned: the world is continuously reinventing itself and we are allowed— even obligated— to participate in the reinvention. They haven’t yet absorbed the anesthetic of cynicism. When Juniper draws a bird, the bird has twelve wings and laser eyes because why not? The bird is not a representation of a bird. It is a new species being born in real time. I watch her and remember that imagination is not escape. It is civic duty. A culture that loses its ability to imagine better worlds is a culture preparing its own coffin.

This leads me, in the way that only free writing can, to the subject of coffins and what we put in them.

Not literal corpses. Metaphorical ones. We bury dreams, friendships, versions of ourselves with startling regularity. The graveyard inside each of us is vast. Some coffins are tiny— the novel we stopped writing at page 47. Others are enormous— the belief that our parents would eventually see us clearly. The healthiest people I know are the ones who visit their internal graveyard regularly but do not live there. They bring flowers. They say the names out loud. Then they walk back into the sunlight and plant something new.

I have been trying to get better at this. For years I treated my failures like toxic waste that had to be hidden in deep geological storage. Now I’m attempting to compost them. The difference is enormous. Compost turns death into soil. Toxic waste just leaks into the groundwater and poisons everything downstream. The older I get, the more I believe that emotional composting is the central skill of adulthood. Everything else— career, relationships, creative practice— is downstream from it.

Speaking of creative practice, let’s talk about the terrifying freedom of having no assignment.

Most of my professional life has been spent fulfilling other people’s briefs. Write this article. Deliver that talk. Make the brand voice sound like a friendly but slightly anxious uncle. There is dignity in good craftsmanship, of course. But there is also a special kind of loneliness that comes from spending decades speaking in other people’s voices. This piece— this 2500-word wander with no brief— feels like coming up for air after years underwater. I didn’t realize how much I was gasping.

The page is the only place where I consistently tell the truth. Not the factual truth. The emotional truth. The difference matters. Facts are clean. Emotional truth is covered in dirt and blood and cake frosting. It contradicts itself. It changes its mind mid-sentence. It uses too many metaphors and then apologizes for using too many metaphors. Good. Let it be messy. The mess is where the life is.

I have been reading a lot of poetry lately, which is dangerous because it ruins you for ordinary language. When you spend time with someone like Marie Howe or Ross Gay, you begin to see that every moment contains a universe if you slow down enough to notice. The way light falls on a banana peel. The particular sound your father makes when he clears his throat. These are not background details. They are the whole story, if you know how to read them.

Ross Gay wrote that joy and pain are not opposites but “magnificent twins.” I think about that every time I watch my daughter laugh until she cries or cry until she laughs. The membrane between the two states is impossibly thin. We spend so much energy trying to stay on the joy side of the membrane, but the membrane itself is where everything interesting happens. It is where art is made. It is where love becomes possible. It is where a middle-aged writer sits down with no plan and ends up crying at his desk because he accidentally wrote the sentence “my daughter is six” and realized how temporary that number is.

Time is the final landmark. I keep returning to it because I can’t escape it.

We are all living inside a slow-motion explosion. The Big Bang is still happening— the universe is still expanding— and we are tiny sparks riding the shockwave, pretending we have permanent addresses. Everything is moving away from everything else at 73 kilometers per second per megaparsec. The only thing that slows the expansion down is gravity, which is to say, love. Not romantic love. The larger love. The love that makes you text your friend at 2 a.m. when you know they’re struggling. The love that makes you plant trees you will never sit under. The love that makes you write 2500 words simply because someone said “write freely” and your soul took it as permission to finally speak.

I don’t know if any of this coheres. I’m not sure it’s supposed to. Coherence is overrated. Life itself is a long experimental poem with no consistent meter. Sometimes it rhymes. Sometimes it dissolves into pure sound. The best we can do is keep listening.

There is a story I love about the physicist Richard Feynman. Late in his life, he was asked by a student what he would do if he had only one day left to live. Feynman thought for a moment and said, “I’d go to the beach. I’d draw a line in the sand. Then I’d dare the ocean to cross it.”

That is how I want to live. Not defiantly, exactly. Playfully. With the full knowledge that the ocean will absolutely cross the line, probably within thirty seconds, but that the drawing of the line was never about winning. It was about declaring temporary but total allegiance to the act of creation. To making a mark. To saying: for one brief moment, I was here, and I noticed everything.

The fog is rolling in again outside my window as I write this. It has that same theatrical quality I remember from childhood. The streetlights are moons. The world feels negotiable. My daughter is asleep upstairs, dreaming whatever six-year-olds dream— probably birds with laser eyes eating ice cream in heaven. My wife is reading a novel in the next room. The music has stopped but the silence feels composed.

I have written 2487 words. Close enough.

If you’ve stayed with me this long, thank you. I hope something in this wandering constellation caught light in your own chest. I hope you draw your own line in the sand tomorrow, even knowing the tide is coming. I hope you fall through the crust of ordinary life into the architecture of wonder that was waiting beneath your feet the entire time.

The fog is beautiful tonight. I think I’ll go stand in it for a while.

(Word count: 2498)

samples.result:
I want to write about the quiet, stubborn beauty of ordinary things.

There is a peculiar comfort in noticing what most people rush past. A cracked sidewalk with a dandelion pushing through. The way steam curls off a bowl of soup like it’s whispering secrets. The soft mechanical click of a turn signal in an empty parking lot at dusk. These are not dramatic moments. They don’t get songs written about them. Yet they contain an entire universe if you slow down enough to let them speak.

I have been thinking lately about how modernity trains us to discard the small. Our phones vibrate with urgent news every few minutes. Algorithms feed us escalating spectacles—larger fires, louder arguments, more cinematic disasters—until the scale of what feels “important” becomes grotesque. In that environment, the small becomes almost rebellious. To sit on a park bench and watch pigeons argue over a crust of bread is a tiny act of civil disobedience against the empire of scale.

There’s a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I keep returning to. It celebrates imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. A chipped teacup that has been lovingly repaired with gold lacquer (*kintsugi*) is more beautiful precisely because it is broken. The repair marks its history rather than hiding it. I wonder what it would look like to apply that philosophy not just to objects but to our lives. To stop apologizing for the cracks. To let the gold fill them instead of pretending the fracture never happened.

Last spring I started taking walks without headphones for the first time in years. The silence felt violent at first. My brain kept reaching for dopamine hits that weren’t there. But after a week or so something shifted. I began noticing the sound of wind moving through different kinds of leaves—how oak leaves make a deeper, almost leathery rustle while birch leaves sound like delicate paper being shaken. I noticed that birds don’t just sing; they have dialects. The crows near my apartment have a particular three-note call that the crows two neighborhoods over don’t seem to use. Local cultures exist even at the level of corvids.

There is a radical humility in admitting how much is happening around us that we never perceive. Scientists estimate that humans are consciously aware of perhaps 0.0004% of the information our senses are taking in at any given moment. The rest is filtered, compressed, discarded. We walk through a world that is shouting at us in frequencies we’ve taught ourselves to ignore.

I’ve been trying to unlearn that compression algorithm.

Some days this takes the form of lying on the floor of my apartment and simply listening. Not meditating. Not trying to achieve anything. Just listening to the layered sounds of the building—refrigerator hum, distant traffic, the occasional creak of floorboards as my neighbor moves around upstairs. There is an entire symphony in what we dismiss as background noise. The French composer Pierre Schaeffer built an entire musical philosophy (*musique concrète*) around this idea—that any sound, removed from its context, can become music. A train whistle. A spinning washing machine. The wet click of someone eating an apple. Once you start hearing this way, it’s hard to stop.

I wonder if this is part of why so many of us feel exhausted. We are asked to live at the speed of fiber optic cables while our nervous systems evolved to track the movement of deer through tall grass. The mismatch creates a kind of spiritual jet lag that no amount of productivity hacking seems able to cure. The cure, if there is one, might be embarrassingly simple: fewer things, more attention.

There’s a story I love about the poet Wendell Berry. Someone asked him what he thought about computers. Berry, who writes longhand and farms with horses, gave what might be the most perfect answer I’ve ever heard: “I would not want to live in a world where I couldn’t throw a rock and hit a pig.” The line works on so many levels. It’s funny. It’s specific. But mostly it’s a declaration of allegiance to a particular scale of existence. A world small enough, tangible enough, that you can still participate in it physically. A world where consequences are visible and responsibility is not abstract.

I think we’re starving for that kind of visibility.

Modern life specializes in making consequences invisible. The clothes we wear, the food we eat, the energy that powers our devices—all of it arrives stripped of its story. We have engineered a reality where the violence and beauty embedded in every object is laundered out before it reaches us. The price of this convenience is a pervasive feeling that nothing is quite real. That we are living in a simulation that has been optimized for engagement rather than meaning.

The antidote isn’t necessarily to abandon modernity. I’m typing these words on a laptop, after all. The antidote might be something closer to double vision—learning to see both the miraculous convenience and the hidden cost at the same time. To hold the contradiction without looking away.

I’ve been experimenting with what I call “slow witness.” The rules are simple. Once a day, I choose something ordinary and give it my complete attention for ten full minutes. No phone. No agenda. Just looking, listening, smelling, touching. A houseplant. A kitchen knife. The pattern of light on a wall. The results have been startling. Things begin to unfold. A single leaf contains galaxies of texture. The way a knife balances in your hand tells you something about every person who ever used it. Even the most mundane objects turn out to have personalities if you give them time.

There is a concept in psychology called “attention restoration theory” which suggests that natural environments have the ability to replenish our directed attention because they engage what’s called “soft fascination.” A river doesn’t demand anything from you. It doesn’t have an agenda. It simply flows, and in doing so it gives your exhausted executive function a chance to rest. I think this applies to more than just nature. Any object or phenomenon approached without agenda can become restorative. The key is the absence of extraction. You’re not trying to mine the moment for content or productivity. You’re simply keeping it company.

This feels almost subversive in 2025.

We live in an economy that has monetized every second of human attention. Even our rest has become performative—optimized sleep scores, mindfulness apps that track your “zen,” vacations carefully documented for social approval. The idea that you might simply sit with something for no reason at all feels like a glitch in the matrix. But maybe that’s exactly why it matters. Every unrecorded, unshared, unoptimized moment of genuine presence becomes a small act of reclamation.

I’ve started collecting what I think of as “useless knowledge.” Not facts that will help me win arguments or advance my career. Just things that feel beautiful or strange enough to be worth remembering. Did you know that octopuses have three hearts? Two pump blood through the gills while the third pumps it through the rest of the body. When an octopus swims, the systemic heart actually stops beating, which is why they prefer crawling. They quite literally find swimming exhausting. I don’t know what practical use this information has, but it makes me happy every time I think about it. The world is so much weirder and more specific than we usually allow ourselves to notice.

There are entire libraries of this kind of knowledge hiding in plain sight. The way bees communicate the location of flowers through dance. The fact that a group of flamingos is called a “stand” while a group of crows is called a “murder.” That slime molds can solve mazes and anticipate future events despite having no brain. That trees in a forest communicate through underground fungal networks, sending warnings about insects or sharing nutrients with sick neighbors. The more you learn, the more the boundary between animate and inanimate starts to feel like a polite fiction we invented to make ourselves feel separate.

Perhaps that’s what I’m really circling around in all of this—the illusion of separateness.

There is a profound loneliness that comes with believing you are a isolated mind moving through a dead universe of objects. But the longer I pay attention, the harder it becomes to maintain that story. Everything seems to be in conversation with everything else. The bacteria in my gut influencing my mood. The moon moving ocean tides that in turn shape coastal ecosystems that support the fish I eat that becomes part of my body. The carbon atoms in my left hand were probably once part of a dinosaur. Nothing is truly separate. We are all just the universe experiencing itself from billions of different angles simultaneously.

This realization doesn’t have to be mystical. It can be as simple as noticing that your breathing is connected to the photosynthesis of plants which is connected to the sun which is connected to the gravitational dance of the entire solar system. When you follow any thread long enough, you end up holding the whole tapestry.

I think this might be what certain spiritual traditions have been trying to tell us in their various languages. Not that we need to transcend the physical world, but that we need to finally see it clearly for the first time. To stop skimming the surface and actually meet reality on its own terms.

There’s a phrase I encountered recently that I can’t stop thinking about: “the ministry of paying attention.” It suggests that careful observation itself can be a form of service. That simply witnessing something with love and presence is enough. You don’t need to fix it or film it or turn it into content. Your attention is already a form of relationship.

I wonder what the world would look like if more of us took this ministry seriously. If we brought the same quality of attention to a neighborhood tree that we bring to our closest relationships. If we treated rainwater, bread dough, street cats, and elderly neighbors as equally worthy of our notice. Not in some forced, exhausting way. But with the natural curiosity we had as children before someone taught us what was “important.”

Children are the patron saints of this kind of attention. They haven’t yet learned to filter. They will spend twenty minutes watching a snail cross a sidewalk with the same focus an adult might bring to closing a million-dollar deal. Their questions reveal how much we’ve stopped seeing: *Why is the moon following us? What does the color blue taste like? Where do shadows go when it gets dark?* We smile at these questions and think they’re cute. We rarely consider that they might be profound.

The older I get, the more I suspect the children are right and the adults have been gaslighting themselves for decades.

I don’t have any grand conclusions to offer. This isn’t that kind of essay. I’m not trying to convince you of anything except perhaps this: the world is still here. It never went anywhere. It’s waiting in the margins, in the cracks, in the spaces between notifications. It’s in the way your coffee mug leaves a perfect circular stain on the table. It’s in the particular rhythm of your neighbor’s footsteps. It’s in the way dust moves in a shaft of afternoon light like it’s performing some private ballet for an audience of one.

All it asks is that you show up without an agenda. That you bring your whole self to the smallest moments. That you let yourself be changed by what you notice instead of trying to extract value from it.

The rewards are not flashy. You won’t suddenly become enlightened or rich or famous. But you might find yourself crying at the sight of moss growing on concrete. You might start talking to houseplants in a serious voice. You might develop an unreasonable affection for a particular patch of sunlight on your floor that moves across the room throughout the day like a slow, faithful pet.

These are not small things.

In a world that measures everything by scale and spectacle, the decision to love what is small, imperfect, and local might be the most radical choice available to us. It is a way of saying: I refuse to outsource my attention to machines. I refuse to let my sense of wonder be determined by what trends on the internet. I choose to remain a citizen of this particular place, this particular time, with these particular flawed and miraculous details.

The dandelion in the sidewalk crack is not waiting for you to notice it. It is already complete. But if you do stop—if you crouch down and really look at how it has engineered its leaves to capture maximum sunlight while surviving being stepped on—you might feel something in your chest loosen that you didn’t know was tight.

That loosening is the beginning.

I have 312 words left to reach 2500. So let me tell you about the time I watched a spider build a web at 3 a.m. during a particularly bad bout of insomnia.

I had given up on sleep and was sitting by the window drinking tea when I noticed movement in the corner of the glass. A tiny spider, no bigger than a fingernail, was methodically constructing an orb web between the window frame and a houseplant. What struck me wasn’t just the engineering feat—though that was impressive enough—but the absolute certainty with which it worked. There was no hesitation, no existential crisis about whether web-building was the right career choice. It simply did what it was made to do with total commitment.

I watched for over an hour as it spun radial lines, then spiral threads, then the sticky catching spiral. At one point it seemed to test the tension of certain strands, plucking them like a musician tuning an instrument. When a moth eventually flew into the web at dawn, the spider moved with such decisive grace that I found myself inexplicably moved. Not because the moth died—I’m not that sentimental—but because the entire sequence felt like witnessing a perfect expression of purpose. The spider didn’t need motivation quotes or life coaching. It had silk and instinct and that was enough.

I think we all secretly long for that kind of clarity about our own function. Not in some reductive capitalist sense of “what do you produce,” but in the deeper sense of alignment between what we are and what we do. The spider doesn’t wonder if it would be happier as a different kind of spider. It doesn’t scroll through other spiders’ perfectly curated web photos and feel inadequate. It simply spins.

There’s something to learn there.

The sun came up while I was watching. The web, previously nearly invisible, suddenly lit up with rainbow refractions as dew formed on the threads. For ten minutes it was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen. Then the spider ate part of its own web (they recycle the silk) and started over in a slightly different location. No attachment. No mourning for the destroyed masterpiece. Just the next necessary thing.

I fell asleep shortly after and dreamed about geometry made of light.

When I woke up I felt different. Not transformed, exactly. But slightly more porous. More willing to let the world surprise me. More aware that miracles happen constantly at scales we rarely notice—in spider silk, in bacterial communication, in the way bread rises, in the particular way someone you love says your name.

I’ve been chasing that feeling ever since. Not constantly. That would be its own form of violence. But regularly enough that it has become a kind of practice. A secular prayer consisting of nothing but showing up and looking carefully at what is already here.

Two hundred and fifty words remain.

Let me use them to say this plainly:

The world is singing at us in frequencies both ancient and new. Most of us have forgotten how to listen. But the song is patient. It waits in half-empty teacups and the smell of rain on hot pavement and the way certain songs make your throat tight for reasons you can’t explain. It waits in the courage it takes to say “I don’t know” and mean it. It waits in the decision to be kind when you could be right.

You don’t need permission to start listening again. You don’t need a special certification or a spiritual teacher or better WiFi. You only need to decide that your attention is worth protecting. That the small, local, specific details of your actual life deserve the same quality of presence you so easily give to disasters and celebrities and other people’s opinions.

Begin anywhere.

Begin with the way light falls across your desk right now. Begin with the sound of your own breathing. Begin with the particular way your favorite mug feels in your hands. Begin stupidly and small and with no plan. The world will meet you there. It always does.

The rest is just paying attention.
