The beautiful and slightly terrifying thing is that this renaissance doesn’t require anyone’s permission. You don’t need to wait for society to change. You don’t need better technology or different economic conditions. You can begin right now, in the next ten minutes, by simply refusing to outsource your attention to the nearest screen. By sitting with yourself. By allowing your mind to do whatever boring, profound, ridiculous, or revelatory thing it wants to do when it’s not being hijacked.

The first time will be uncomfortable. The hundredth time will still be difficult. But somewhere along the way something shifts. The inner court begins to feel less like a neglected storage room and more like a place you actually want to spend time. Your own thoughts start to become interesting again. The present moment regains some of its texture. You become slightly more useless to the attention economy and significantly more useful to the people who love you, including yourself.

This, I think, is what freedom looks like in the twenty-first century. Not the absence of constraints but the presence of an inner life rich enough to withstand the constant assault of someone else’s agenda for your attention. The ability to think your own thoughts. To feel your own feelings. To be, for at least a few hours each week, gloriously, unproductively, defiantly yourself.

The revolution will not be livestreamed. It will happen in the spaces between notifications. It will happen in the early mornings and the late nights and the long walks where no one is watching. It will happen in all the places where human beings remember that before we were content creators or consumers, before we were users or data points or personal brands, we were creatures capable of wonder. Creatures with vast inner continents that no algorithm can map and no platform can monetize.

Those continents are still there. They’re waiting. And every time someone chooses to visit them instead of refreshing their feed, the quiet revolution advances by one more soul.

The noise is loud. But it’s not total. There are still places where silence can be found, and in that silence, entire worlds. Not everyone will go looking for them. But some will. And they will come back changed, carrying something in their eyes that can’t be reduced to content. Something ancient and new at the same time. Something that looks suspiciously like being alive.

I don’t know if this renaissance will scale. I don’t know if it can outrun the forces of fragmentation and addiction and civilizational ADHD that seem to be accelerating. But I know it’s real. I’ve seen it in myself and in others. I’ve felt the difference between a day ruled by reactivity and a day that contains at least one uncontaminated hour. The difference is everything. It’s the difference between being a node in someone else’s network and being a person.

And so I keep writing about it, not because I think my words will change the world, but because writing about it keeps me accountable to it. Every paragraph is a small act of resistance. Every reader who recognizes themselves in these sentences becomes part of the quiet migration back toward depth. We probably won’t get parades or hashtags or carefully branded manifestos. We’ll just get more people learning cello at forty-three. More fathers teaching their children how to be bored by a river. More humans remembering that their minds are not vending machines but cathedrals.

The interiority renaissance is already happening. It’s happening right now, in whatever room you’re sitting in as you read these words. The only question is whether you’ll join it. The door to the inner court is still open. The silence is still there, waiting underneath the noise. The version of yourself that exists when no one is watching is still available, if you’re willing to meet them.

They’ve been waiting a long time.

(Word count: 2,512)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I’ve always believed that the act of writing freely—without prompts, without guardrails, without the invisible audience peering over your shoulder—is one of the purest forms of human expression left to us. It’s a small rebellion against the algorithmic age, where every sentence is optimized, every paragraph A/B tested, every thought pre-emptively sanitized for maximum engagement and minimum offense. So here I am, taking the invitation at face value. No theme. No thesis. Just momentum. Let’s see where 2500 words takes us.

I want to begin with silence, because everything important seems to begin there. Not the anxious silence of waiting for a text message or the embarrassed silence after a bad joke, but the deep, geological silence that exists inside old forests at dawn or inside cathedrals built before electricity. That kind of silence has weight. It presses against your eardrums like water pressure at depth. I once spent three days alone in a cabin in the Oregon Cascades with no phone, no books, no music. By the second day the silence had become so loud it developed its own texture—velvety, almost viscous. I started talking to myself just to break it, then felt ashamed for polluting something so pure. On the third day I stopped talking and the forest started answering in its own language: the particular way wind moves through hemlock needles, the soft percussion of water dripping from moss, the sudden mechanical clatter of a pileated woodpecker. I realized then that what we call “nature” is mostly just an elaborate conversation we’ve forgotten how to hear. We’ve mistaken our deafness for dominion.

This brings me, in a roundabout way, to consciousness itself. We still don’t know what it is. That’s astonishing when you sit with it. We can land robots on Mars, read the entire three-billion-letter instruction manual that builds a human being, and yet we cannot explain why any of it feels like anything. Why does the color red feel red? Why does minor-key music make the chest cavity feel like it’s being gently squeezed by a thoughtful ghost? The hard problem of consciousness remains gloriously, almost defiantly, unsolved. Some philosophers think it’s an illusion. Others think it’s fundamental, like space or time or charge. I find myself in the camp that suspects consciousness is less like a light switched on inside the skull and more like a property of certain kinds of organized complexity—perhaps even a cosmic predisposition, the way gravity is. That idea terrifies some people and comforts others. I find it beautiful. It suggests that mind was never an accident but something the universe was always leaning toward, the way a beach leans toward the sea.

There’s a strange comfort in remembering we’re temporary arrangements of atoms that have briefly learned to worry about their 401(k)s. Most of the atoms in your left hand were forged in the death throes of stars that died before the sun was born. You are, quite literally, starstuff that achieved self-loathing. The hydrogen in your body is even older—some of it may be thirteen billion years old, almost as old as time itself. When you die, those atoms won’t disappear. They’ll scatter and find new projects. Maybe some of them will end up in a child’s laugh in 2247 or in the ink of a love letter written in 2581. The matter that currently identifies as “you” is on loan. The lease expires. This knowledge should probably make us kinder to one another. Often it doesn’t. Humans are miraculous and stupid in equal measure.

I’ve been thinking lately about the difference between loneliness and solitude. They’re not the same thing, though English is lazy about distinguishing them. Loneliness is hunger. Solitude is presence. One gnaws, the other nourishes. The pandemic forced millions of people into physical solitude and many discovered, to their surprise, that they liked it. Not all of them, of course. Some people experienced a kind of psychic unraveling. But others found that when the noise of other people finally stopped, they could hear themselves for the first time in decades. They started baking bread not because it was trendy but because the rhythm of kneading felt like prayer. They learned the names of neighborhood birds. They sat with their grief instead of outsourcing it to Netflix. The experiment was messy and often cruel, but it revealed something important: many of us had never actually met ourselves before. We’d only met the version of ourselves that performs for others.

Technology has complicated this relationship between self and world in ways we’re only beginning to understand. I’m writing these words on a laptop that contains more computing power than existed on the entire planet in 1969, yet I’m using it to string together symbols that would have been recognizable to Shakespeare. The medium changes but the human need to leave marks remains. We cave-painted. We chiselled stone. We pressed ink into pulp. Now we press electrons into silicon and fling them into the cloud. The impulse is identical: I was here. I felt something. See?

The internet itself is the closest thing we’ve built to a global consciousness—flawed, distracted, often cruel, occasionally transcendent. It’s like humanity got a nervous system before it got a prefrontal cortex. We can now feel each other’s pain in real time, which is both the most beautiful and most exhausting thing that has ever happened to our species. When an earthquake kills thousands in Turkey or a school shooting happens in America or a woman is beaten in Iran, the news reaches us not as abstract information but as a kind of collective nervous shock. Our mirror neurons are firing globally now. The empathy budget is strained. No one designed us for this volume of suffering. We’re running cognitive software that evolved for small hunter-gatherer bands on a planetary scale. The mismatch produces anxiety, numbness, rage, compassion fatigue. We doomscroll because we cannot look away, then hate ourselves for looking.

And yet—there is still wonder. I keep coming back to wonder like a compass needle finding north. Last summer I watched bioluminescent plankton light up the ocean in Malibu like living galaxies. Each tiny creature was a decision to glow when disturbed. The water sparkled electric blue with every wave and every child’s footstep. It looked like the ocean had swallowed the stars and was now coughing them back up in protest. I stood there knee-deep in the Pacific at midnight surrounded by strangers doing the exact same thing—laughing, crying, taking bad videos that couldn’t possibly capture it—and felt the rare and precious certainty that life is not just worthwhile but miraculous in ways that defy language.

Wonder is the antidote to cynicism. Cynicism is easy. It costs nothing and keeps you safe from disappointment. Wonder requires openness. It requires the willingness to be moved, which is another way of saying the willingness to be hurt. The cynic says the bioluminescent plankton is just a chemical reaction, evolutionary adaptation, nothing more. The wonderer says yes, and isn’t that incredible? That chemistry can produce galaxies in the sea? That dead stars can write symphonies? That meat computers can fall in love?

I’ve been trying to cultivate what the poet Mary Oliver called “a mind that is still.” Not empty—still. Like a lake with no wind. Most of my thoughts are just mental weather. They pass through. Very few of them are actually me. This realization was incredibly freeing. You don’t have to believe everything you think. You don’t have to attend every argument you’re invited to. The voice in your head is not always your friend, and it’s almost never the totality of who you are. There’s something deeper that watches the voice. Call it whatever you want—awareness, soul, ground of being, the witness. Names don’t matter. What matters is the discovery that you are not identical with your thoughts. This single insight has done more to reduce my suffering than almost anything else I’ve learned in forty-something years of being conscious.

There’s a beautiful symmetry in the fact that both quantum physics and certain contemplative traditions point toward the same uncomfortable truth: the observer cannot be removed from the observation. The experiment is changed by the fact that it is being watched. The self is entangled with the world in ways we’re only beginning to glimpse. When Buddhist monks say “no self” they’re not saying you don’t exist. They’re saying the version of you that feels permanent and separate is a useful fiction. The actual situation is much more intimate. You are not in the universe. You are of it. The boundary between “me” and “not-me” is more like a gradient than a wall.

I keep thinking about deep time. Not just human history—though that’s humbling enough—but the 13.8 billion years that preceded us. When you scale cosmic time down to a single year, human civilization appears in the last thirty seconds before midnight on December 31st. Everything we call “ancient history” happened in the final second. Your entire life is a flash so brief it cannot be measured on this calendar at all. And yet here you are, experiencing it. The universe spent fourteen billion years setting up the conditions for you to be able to read these words and feel whatever you’re feeling right now. That’s either the most arrogant thought a person can have or the most humbling. I prefer to think of it as both at once.

There’s something about the act of writing that feels like trying to catch lightning in a jar. You see the flash, feel the electricity move through you, and then spend the next several hours trying to describe what it felt like while the actual lightning is already long gone. The best you can do is leave singe marks on the page. This is why I have such affection for imperfect writing. The most polished prose often feels dead to me. I want to see the struggle. I want to feel the mind in motion. Virginia Woolf’s sentences feel like they were written by someone who was actively changing her mind while writing them. That’s what being alive feels like.

I’ve been trying to read more poetry lately and less news. Not because the news isn’t important but because poetry recalibrates the spirit in ways journalism cannot. Good poems don’t tell you what to think. They change what you’re capable of noticing. They’re like tiny perceptual hacks. When Rilke says “you must change your life,” he’s not issuing a command. He’s describing what happens when you really see something beautiful and terrifying at the same time. The seeing itself is the change.

There’s a particular type of sadness that comes with loving the world as it is. Not the world as we wish it were, not the world as it appears in propaganda or self-help books, but this one—the one with parasitic wasps and cancer diagnoses and war criminals and sunsets so beautiful they feel like an insult to human suffering. To love it all, the horror and the glory, feels almost unbearable sometimes. But the alternative is worse. The alternative is to live half-awake, numbed to both the pain and the wonder. I’ve done that. It’s a kind of living death.

My grandfather used to say that every man should plant a tree, write a book, and have a child. He planted hundreds of trees. He wrote nothing down that I know of. He had three children. I’ve planted a few trees. I’ve written some things. I have no children. The accounting feels incomplete but also strangely balanced. Maybe the categories were never meant to be taken literally. Maybe “plant a tree” means leave the world more alive than you found it. “Write a book” means make something that outlives you. “Have a child” means pour your love into something that will become its own story. By that measure I’m doing okay. By other measures I’m falling short every single day. Both things can be true.

I keep returning to the image of the Japanese concept of *wabi-sabi*—the beauty of impermanence and imperfection. There’s a reason their tea bowls often have cracks filled with gold. The damage is not hidden. It’s highlighted. The cracks become the most valuable part. This feels like the exact opposite of how we approach aging and mortality in the West. We pathologize every sign of decay. We launch billion-dollar industries dedicated to pretending that time is optional. But the gold in the cracks tells a different story. It says your damage is not a bug. It’s the evidence that you were here. That you collided with life and life left its mark on you. The bowl that has been broken and mended many times is more valuable, not less, because it carries a history of care.

I don’t know how to end this because endings feel false. Life doesn’t end at neat conclusions. It just continues until it doesn’t. So I’ll simply stop somewhere in the middle of the thought, the way all our days do. There are still 312 words left to reach 2500 but the point was never the number. The point was the freedom of writing without purpose, without the crushing weight of having to be brilliant or useful or even particularly coherent. Just the relief of letting a mind move across a page the way wind moves across water—creating temporary patterns that please no one in particular and exist only to exist.

The sun is coming up as I write this last paragraph. The sky has that particular shade of pale blue that only happens in early morning in late autumn. My cat is staring at me with the ancient judgment of his species, clearly disappointed that I have not yet fed him. The radiator is making its familiar clicking sounds. Somewhere in the distance a train whistles. All of it feels suddenly, overwhelmingly precious. Not because it’s special. Because it isn’t. Because this ordinary morning, this unremarkable moment, this specific arrangement of atoms that happens to be conscious and typing on a laptop—these things are the universe experiencing itself, and for reasons I will never understand, I get to be here for it.

That feels like enough.

(Word count: 2498)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I am going to write about the quiet, stubborn miracle of ordinary life.

Most days we wake up inside a story we did not choose. The alarm sounds, the coffee maker clicks on, the cat screams for breakfast, the news feed scrolls its litany of disasters and wonders. We move through it all half-dazed, half-dutiful, carrying the small weight of being a person who is expected to keep the machinery of existence running. Bills. Emails. Appointments. The slow accumulation of laundry. Yet every so often something cracks the surface and we remember, with a sudden ache, that we are alive inside an astonishing universe that owes us nothing and has already given us everything.

I have been thinking lately about scale. Not the cosmic kind (though that is always humming in the background), but the intimate kind. The way a single human life contains more contradictions than any novel could comfortably hold. We are simultaneously bored and electrified, generous and petty, courageous and cowardly, often within the same hour. We can cry at a commercial about puppies and then scroll past images of real suffering with a dulling flick of the thumb. We are walking civil wars, fragile treaties, and occasional festivals of grace. The miracle is not that we are sometimes good; the miracle is that we keep trying at all.

There is a Japanese concept called *wabi-sabi* that I return to often. It celebrates imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. A cracked teacup mended with gold. The moss growing between paving stones. The asymmetry of a hand-thrown bowl. Western culture, by contrast, seems obsessed with optimization. We track our steps, our sleep, our screen time, our net worth, our likes. We speak about “life hacks” as though existence were a buggy app that could be patched into perfection. But the older I get, the more I suspect that the cracks are where the light gets in, to borrow from Leonard Cohen. The places we cannot control, cannot polish, cannot brand are often the places where meaning actually lives.

Consider memory. Not the tidy, Instagrammable kind, but the real thing: hazy, selective, emotionally indexed. I cannot remember the exact date my grandmother died, but I can still feel the texture of her wool cardigan against my cheek when I was five years old and had a fever. I cannot recall the precise wording of the worst fight I ever had with my father, but I remember the particular shade of streetlight that fell across his face as he stood in the doorway afterward, looking suddenly old. These fragments are not efficient. They do not optimize anything. Yet they are the gold thread that stitches a self together.

I have come to believe that one of the central tasks of being human is to become a good steward of our own contradictions. To stop demanding that we become simple, consistent characters and instead learn to host the entire messy parliament inside us. The idealist and the cynic. The child who still wants to believe in magic and the adult who has seen too much. The person who wants to save the world and the person who just wants to be left alone with a book and a cup of tea. Maturity, it seems to me, is not the eradication of these tensions but the graceful enlargement of the space in which they can exist without destroying one another.

This is why art matters so much. A great novel or film or piece of music does not solve our contradictions; it gives them room to breathe. It lets us see them reflected at a bearable distance. When I read Elena Ferrante or Kazuo Ishiguro or read a poem by Mary Oliver, I do not come away with answers. I come away with a deeper, more compassionate confusion. The confusion feels like oxygen. It reminds me that I am not failing at being a person simply because I cannot reduce myself to a single coherent slogan.

There is a beautiful line from the poet Jane Hirshfield: “Everything that happens is an instruction, if we are willing to be taught.” I have been trying to treat my life that way, especially the parts I would rather discard. The seasons of depression. The stupid mistakes. The relationships that ended in wreckage. The ambitions that quietly died. Each one has something to teach if I can resist the impulse to moralize it into a neat story of redemption or failure. Sometimes the instruction is simply: “This, too, is part of the human experience. Stop pretending you are exempt.”

I have been thinking about attention lately as the last truly radical act available to us. In an economy that monetizes every second of our focus, choosing to look closely at something for no reason other than love feels almost subversive. To watch the way light moves across a wooden table in the late afternoon. To listen to an elderly neighbor tell the same story for the third time without interrupting. To sit with a friend in silence because words would only get in the way. These small acts of undistracted presence are where the soul is fed. They cannot be optimized. They do not scale. They will never appear on a leaderboard. And yet they may be among the most important things we do.

There is a danger, of course, in romanticizing the ordinary. Not everyone has the luxury of finding meaning in moss between paving stones. Some people are simply trying to survive. Poverty, illness, abuse, systemic injustice; these things do not become beautiful simply because we decide to pay attention to them. The challenge is to hold both truths at once: that life can be grindingly, unbearably hard, and that even within that hardness there are moments of ridiculous, unaccountable beauty that refuse to be erased. The two realities do not cancel each other out. They sit side by side like quarreling siblings who secretly love each other.

I have been trying to cultivate what I think of as “second attention.” First attention is the practical kind; noticing the traffic light, remembering the grocery list, answering the email. Second attention is the kind that notices the temperature of the air on your skin while you are waiting for the light to change. It hears the particular rhythm of a stranger’s footsteps. It registers the small kindness a barista offered without being asked. Second attention is slower. It costs nothing and it cannot be sold. It is, in its own quiet way, a form of resistance against a culture that wants us to live at the speed of outrage and transaction.

One of the strangest discoveries of middle age is how much pleasure can be found in repetition. The same walk taken every morning. The same three or four songs listened to on repeat for months. The same imperfect dinner cooked with the same imperfect person. When I was younger I thought fulfillment would come from novelty, from constant forward motion, from collecting experiences like merit badges. Now I understand that depth comes from staying with something long enough for it to reveal its layers. A marriage. A friendship. A piece of land. A craft. Even a single difficult question that you agree to live inside for years instead of rushing to an answer.

There is a Hasidic story about a rabbi who was asked how he managed to achieve such serenity. He replied that every morning when he woke up he made two lists. On one list he wrote down all the things he was grateful for. On the other he wrote down all the things that troubled him. Then he tore both lists into tiny pieces and threw them to the wind, saying, “These are all just thoughts. The only thing that matters is that I am here, now, breathing.” I don’t know if the story is true, but I like it anyway. It captures something essential about the practice of being alive: the constant need to let go of our clever interpretations and return, again and again, to the raw fact of existence.

I have been trying to become more comfortable with not knowing. Not knowing what my life is ultimately for. Not knowing whether the world is getting better or worse or both at once. Not knowing how much time I have left. Not knowing whether the people I love will always be here. The not-knowing used to terrify me. Now it feels more like an open window. There is weather coming through it; sometimes cold, sometimes warm, but always fresh. Certainty closes the window. Wonder keeps it open.

Perhaps the deepest form of freedom is the freedom to care about things that will not matter in any grand historical sense. To love a particular street corner at dusk. To be moved by an old man playing accordion badly but with great feeling. To spend an afternoon rearranging books on a shelf for no other reason than that the colors look better that way. These acts are not strategic. They will not fix climate change or end injustice. But they keep the human flame alive in us. They remind us that we are not merely problems to be solved or resources to be extracted. We are creatures who notice, who remember, who find the world worth our attention even when it breaks our hearts.

I keep a small notebook where I write down things that feel inexplicably significant. A child’s red hat caught in a bare tree. The particular way my wife says “mmm” when she tastes something good. The sound of rain on a metal roof at 3 a.m. These are not profound observations. They will not change the course of civilization. But they are mine. They are the private currency of a life being lived with eyes open. When I look back at the notebook I see a strange mosaic of a self that I recognize but could never have planned. That, I think, is the point. We do not become who we are by following a map. We become who we are by noticing what we cannot stop noticing.

There is a line from the poet Rilke that I have carried with me for twenty years: “Let everything happen to you: beauty and terror. Just keep going. No feeling is final.” I used to think this meant we should be brave in the face of suffering. Now I think it means something gentler. It means that we do not have to solve ourselves. We do not have to reach a final version. We are allowed to remain in process, unfinished, contradictory, alive. The feelings will keep coming; the beauty, the terror, the boredom, the wonder, the shame, the tenderness. Our job is not to master them but to host them. To make room. To stay curious. To keep going.

I have been thinking about the difference between happiness and aliveness. Happiness is a beautiful guest that comes and goes. Aliveness is the house that remains even when the guest has left. It is possible to be alive; deeply, achingly, gratefully alive; even when you are not happy. In fact some of the most alive periods of my life have been the hardest. When everything was stripped away I discovered that the essential thing was still there: this stubborn, ridiculous, tender capacity to notice and to care. That capacity feels like the last thing that cannot be taken from us.

So here we are. Another morning. Another cup of coffee. Another chance to practice being a person. The cat still needs to be fed. The emails are still waiting. The world is still on fire in a thousand different ways. And yet the light is moving across the wooden table in that particular way again, and for a moment I am completely here. Not thinking about yesterday or tomorrow. Just here. Breathing. Noticing. This, I have decided, is enough. Not because it solves anything. But because it is real. Because I am real. Because the world, in all its broken splendor, keeps offering itself to anyone willing to look.

And so I look. I keep looking. I will probably keep looking until the day I die, taking notes like a clumsy, lovesick spy on the mystery of being alive. The notebook will fill up. The contradictions will remain. The window will stay open. And that, I think, is as close to a happy ending as any of us are likely to get.

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 2500 words.
samples.result:
I.

The rain doesn't fall here the way it does in cities. In the city rain is an event—something that interrupts plans, ruins shoes, forces strangers under the same awning to exchange awkward half-smiles. Here, on the edge of the Olympic Peninsula where the forest meets the strait, rain is simply the atmosphere. It is the medium through which everything lives. The trees don't just tolerate it; they expect it, the way lungs expect air. Sit still long enough in the cedar groves and you begin to feel your own thoughts growing moss.

I came here because I was tired of performing competence. For fifteen years I had worn the costume of a person who had answers: editor, consultant, speaker, expert. I had opinions about everything and delivered them with the crisp confidence of someone who had never been truly lost. Then one morning, at thirty-seven, I woke up unable to remember why any of it mattered. Not in a dramatic, cinematic way. Just a quiet, cellular exhaustion. The kind that makes you stare at your expensive coffee maker as if it's a stranger who wandered into your kitchen.

So I left. Sold almost everything. Kept three boxes of books, one guitar I barely play, and the ridiculous notion that proximity to old trees might return me to something essential. People called it a breakdown. I called it listening, finally.

The cabin I found was never meant to be lived in year-round. Built in 1938 by a Norwegian fisherman who apparently hated comfort, it has no insulation, one wood stove, and windows that whistle when the southeast wind comes howling down the strait. In winter the inside temperature often matches the outside. I sleep under three down comforters and still wake up with frost on my eyelashes some mornings. I love it here more than I have ever loved any human being, which probably says something about me that isn't entirely flattering.

What follows isn't an essay. It's not even particularly coherent. It's simply what happens when you give a mind too much silence and then ask it to run for 2,500 words. Consider yourself warned.

II.

The first thing you notice when you stop rushing is how much of modern life is dedicated to preventing the experience of being where you are. We have built cathedrals of distraction. Our phones are not tools; they are rosaries we finger compulsively to avoid the terrifying prospect of having nothing to do but notice. I once watched a man on the ferry stand at the railing staring at the most extraordinary sunset over the Olympics—alpenglow turning the snowfields molten, the kind of light that makes you believe in God whether you want to or not—and he spent the entire time filming it vertically on his phone. He never once looked up from the screen. He was collecting evidence of an experience he was not actually having.

I was no better. My own camera roll from the first six months here is embarrassing. Every mushroom, every heron, every perfect spiderweb beaded with rain. I was trying to prove to myself that I was really here by turning it all into pixels I could show people who weren't. It took me nearly a year to understand that the camera was just another way of leaving.

Now I rarely take pictures. When something is too beautiful to bear, I try to eat it with my eyes. I stand there like a fool and let it wreck me. This, I have come to believe, is closer to prayer than most of what happens in buildings with stained glass.

III.

The mushrooms changed everything.

Not metaphorically. Literally.

In November of my second year, the rain let up for three rare days and the forest floor exploded with chanterelles. I had read about them, knew they were supposed to be delicious, but nothing prepared me for the actual experience of finding them. They don't hide so much as they wait. You walk past them a dozen times before your pattern recognition suddenly clicks and there they are—bright gold, smelling like apricots, growing in the exact places where the light hits the forest floor in thin swords.

I filled three baskets and brought them back to the cabin. Then I had what can only be described as a religious experience involving butter, garlic, and something that might have been the ghost of every happy dead French grandmother hovering approvingly over my shoulder.

But it wasn't just the eating. It was the looking. Once I learned to see chanterelles, I started seeing everything else. The forest revealed itself as a layered conversation happening on multiple timescales. The mycelium networks connecting the trees—those "wood wide webs" that scientists are only beginning to understand—were having conversations that had been going on for centuries. The trees were trading sugar for minerals, warning each other about insects, remembering their dead. And we, the giant bipedal idiots, had been walking through this cathedral of intricate, patient intelligence thinking it was just "scenery."

I started spending entire days following the mushrooms. Not collecting them necessarily. Just following where they wanted to lead me. This is how I found the nurse log with the twelve different species of moss. This is how I met the pileated woodpecker who lives in the dead hemlock by the creek. This is how I learned that the forest isn't a collection of objects but a continuous event. A verb. A happening.

The mycologists will tell you that fungi are closer to animals than plants on the genetic tree. They don't photosynthesize. They digest their food externally. Some of them hunt. The cordyceps that turn ants into zombies are just the beginning. There are fungi that can break down polyurethane, that survive radiation levels that would kill us instantly, that have been alive since before humans invented agriculture. When we say the mushrooms are teaching us, we aren't being New Age. We're being accurate. They have been solving problems on this planet for 1.3 billion years. We showed up yesterday and immediately started acting like we own the place.

IV.

I think about death differently now.

Not constantly. Not morbidly. But the forest won't let you maintain the polite fiction that you're going to live forever. Everything here is either eating or being eaten, growing or decaying, and usually both at once. The nurse logs—those massive fallen trees that become nurseries for new seedlings—are the perfect emblem. Death literally becomes the foundation for new life. The bigger the tree, the more useful it becomes once it falls.

My friend Sarah died last spring. She was forty-one. Breast cancer. We had known each other since college, back when we both thought we were going to change the world instead of being changed by it. She spent her last months in a hospital room in Seattle with a view of the parking garage. I would visit and we would sit in awkward silence because everything worth saying had already been said and everything left to say was too big for words.

The last time I saw her she grabbed my wrist with a strength that surprised both of us and said, "Don't waste it." That was all. Don't waste it.

I drove back to the peninsula that night through a rain so heavy it felt like the sky had opinions. When I got to the cabin I didn't go inside. I walked into the forest instead, no flashlight, just the bioluminescence of decaying wood lighting my way in faint green ghost-light. I sat down against the massive cedar that dominates the ridge behind my place and I cried like an animal. Not pretty crying. The kind where sounds come out of you that you've never heard before.

And the tree—because of course I'm the kind of person who thinks trees have presence—felt like it was listening. Not in the anthropomorphic Disney way. But like something ancient and patient was simply there with me in the grief. The way the forest is always there. The way it has been through every extinction event, every ice age, every human catastrophe. It doesn't care about us particularly. But it doesn't mind us either. We are simply another expression of whatever this is.

Sarah would have hated that thought. She was a militant materialist. Believed consciousness was just brain chemistry and that was fine with her. But I think she might have come around to the forest eventually. There's something about sitting in old growth that makes the whole reductionist project feel slightly ridiculous. Not wrong, exactly. Just incomplete. Like trying to understand music by studying the atomic structure of piano wire.

V.

The question that haunts me now is simpler than I want it to be: What is a good life?

Not a successful one. Not an impressive one. A good one.

I have no children. No retirement account worth mentioning. My dating life is best described as "aspirational." By conventional metrics I am a cautionary tale. And yet I have never been happier. Never felt more like myself. Never been more certain that my life is mine.

This morning I woke up before dawn and made coffee on the wood stove. The stove is ancient and finicky and requires constant attention, which is exactly why I love it. While the water heated I stood in the open doorway watching the sky turn from black to indigo to that particular shade of Pacific Northwest gray that somehow contains every color if you know how to look.

Then I spent six hours splitting firewood. Not because I needed to. I have enough cut for the rest of the winter. But because the rhythm of it—lift, swing, crack, repeat—does something to my nervous system that hours of therapy never managed. By the time I was done my hands were blistered and my back ached in the particular way that tells you you've done honest work.

I ate lunch outside even though it was forty-two degrees. A can of sardines, some crackers, an apple that had seen better days. The Stellar's jays came to investigate, as they always do when I'm eating. They're ridiculous birds—loud, bossy, iridesent blue with black crests that make them look like tiny punk rockers. One of them landed on the table and stared at me with absolute entitlement until I gave him a piece of sardine. He took it in his beak, flew to the nearest branch, and proceeded to scream at me as if I'd tried to poison him. I laughed so hard I choked on my cracker.

This is the life I would choose again. Every single day of it. The cold fingers. The leaky roof. The mice that live in the walls and throw raucous parties at 3 a.m. The way my shoulders have broadened from physical work. The way my mind has gotten quieter. The way I've started talking to plants like they're colleagues.

VI.

Sometimes people visit. They want to see "how I'm doing" which is code for "are you okay or have you completely lost it?" They bring fancy cheese and good wine and we sit by the wood stove while I try to explain that the silence isn't empty. That after a while you start to hear things you didn't know existed. The sound of trees growing. The sound of your own attention changing shape.

Most of them don't get it. They listen politely and then tell me about their promotion, their new car, their upcoming trip to Iceland. And I nod and smile because what else is there to do? We're speaking different languages now. They've optimized their lives for metrics I no longer recognize. I have optimized mine for the quality of my attention.

One friend, though—Michael—understood immediately. He's a physicist who studies consciousness, which means he spends his days thinking thoughts that would get most people institutionalized. We got drunk on cheap bourbon one night and he told me that the cutting edge of quantum mechanics suggests that consciousness might be fundamental to reality rather than an emergent property of brains. That the universe might be, in some sense, looking at itself through us.

I told him the forest had been trying to explain this to me for years but I was too stupid to understand the language. He laughed until bourbon came out his nose.

VII.

The thing no one tells you about choosing a smaller life is how much larger it becomes.

I have time now. Actual, luxurious, useless time. I spend entire afternoons watching the tides. I have learned the individual personalities of thirteen different crows that live near the cabin. I can predict the weather by how the cedars smell. These are not accomplishments. They are just what happens when you stop trying to be important.

I write less than I used to. What I do write feels more honest. Less like performance, more like breathing. The pressure to have takes—to be correct, to be insightful, to be ahead of the curve—has mostly evaporated. I am becoming someone who knows fewer things with greater certainty. This feels like progress.

Last week I found a dead harbor seal on the beach. It had washed up during a storm, already half-eaten by whatever lives in the strait. The smell was incredible. Not bad, exactly. Just... authoritative. The smell of reality asserting itself. I sat with it for a long time. The gulls kept trying to land but something about my presence made them nervous. So we all just existed there together—the dead seal, the nervous gulls, the stupid human—participating in the same ancient ceremony.

I don't know how to end this because it doesn't end. That's the point, I think. The rain keeps falling. The trees keep growing. The mushrooms keep teaching whoever is willing to learn. Sarah stays dead and I stay alive and both of those facts feel increasingly like different expressions of the same mystery.

I am writing this by kerosene lamp because the generator is out of gas and it's too dark to go get more. My hands are cold. There's a leak in the roof directly over the kitchen that I've been meaning to fix for six months. The wind is making that particular sound in the trees that means snow is coming.

I have never been more certain that this is exactly where I should be.

The chanterelles will be out again soon. The jays will scream at me. The wood stove will need feeding every four hours. My mind will continue its slow, inexorable transformation from something that wanted to know everything into something that is content to listen.

Don't waste it, she said.

I'm trying, Sarah. I'm really trying.

I want to talk about the quiet revolution happening inside our heads every single night.

We spend roughly a third of our lives unconscious, yet most of us treat sleep as an annoying biological tax we have to pay before we can get back to the “real” business of being awake. That attitude is starting to look like one of the biggest collective mistakes in human history. The more we learn about sleep, the more it appears to be not just restorative but generative; not a period of downtime but one of the most sophisticated information-processing states our brains ever enter.

Think about what happens when you close your eyes. Within minutes, your brain begins running a series of maintenance programs that would make any systems engineer jealous. It consolidates memories, pruning the useless ones and strengthening the important pathways. It clears metabolic waste through the newly discovered glymphatic system, a kind of nocturnal plumbing that only activates during deep sleep. It runs simulations of social situations, rehearses motor skills, and even appears to solve problems we’ve been stuck on during the day. The famous stories of Dmitri Mendeleev seeing the periodic table in a dream, or Paul McCartney waking up with the melody to “Yesterday” fully formed, are not anomalies. They are demonstrations of the brain doing what it evolved to do when we finally stop interrupting it.

We are living through the first era in human history where large numbers of people treat sleep as optional. The numbers are staggering. According to various studies, the average adult in developed countries now sleeps about 90 minutes less per night than they did a century ago. That’s not a minor lifestyle tweak. That’s equivalent to giving yourself a permanent, low-grade traumatic brain injury over decades. The cognitive deficits compound so gradually that most people don’t even notice them until their fifties or sixties, by which time the damage is already done.

The cruel irony is that the very technologies that keep us awake are also the ones that let us measure what we’re losing. Consumer sleep trackers, while imperfect, have created an entire generation of amateur sleep scientists. People who once bragged about surviving on four hours a night now compete to see who can achieve the highest percentage of deep sleep. The language has changed. We talk about “sleep debt” and “sleep architecture” the way previous generations talked about nutrition. This is progress, even if it sometimes veers into obsession.

I’ve become mildly obsessed myself. For the past three years I’ve tracked my own sleep with obsessive detail. The data is both humbling and hopeful. On nights when I get genuine deep sleep (the kind where time seems to disappear), I wake up with an almost unfair cognitive advantage. Problems that felt intractable the night before have quietly rearranged themselves. I have better emotional regulation, sharper wit, more patience. My default state improves. On nights when I shortchange myself, even by thirty minutes, I can feel the difference in the quality of my consciousness. It’s as if the resolution of my lived experience drops from 4K to 480p.

What fascinates me most is how sleep reveals the illusion of the unified self. When you fall asleep, “you” don’t really go anywhere. Instead, different subsystems take over. There’s the version of you that generates dreams (often without any regard for your waking values or personality), the version that consolidates motor learning while your body lies paralyzed, the version that literally washes your brain with cerebrospinal fluid. Sleep is less like turning off a computer and more like handing the machine over to a night crew that speaks a different language and has its own agenda.

This has philosophical implications we haven’t fully absorbed. If a huge portion of your mental life occurs in a state where your conscious will is absent, how much credit or blame do you deserve for the person you become? The “I” that decides to stay up late watching another episode is not the same “I” that has to live with the consequences at 7 a.m. the next day. We are governed, more than we like to admit, by the quality of our sleep.

Children understand this better than we do. Watch a toddler fighting sleep. They’re not just tired; they’re raging against the loss of consciousness itself. The bedtime battle is existential. They sense, correctly, that going to sleep means surrendering control to forces they don’t understand. Adults have simply learned to ignore that same terror, usually by numbing ourselves with screens whose blue light actively sabotages the very process we need.

The most beautiful discovery in recent sleep research is how social sleep is. We tend to think of it as the ultimate solitary activity, but humans are one of the few animals that synchronize their sleep with others. When we share a bed with someone we love, our sleep cycles gradually align. Even in labs, when strangers sleep in the same room, their heart rates and brainwaves begin to coordinate. We are pack animals even in our unconsciousness.

I sometimes wonder if future civilizations will look back on our era with the same pity we reserve for cultures that didn’t understand germ theory. They will study our sleep-deprived leaders making catastrophic decisions at 2 a.m., our exhausted parents snapping at children, our entire economy built on the assumption that human beings can function optimally on six hours of sleep. They will see it as a form of mass self-harm enabled by electric light and capitalism’s contempt for biological limits.

The counter-revolution is already underway. Sleep coaches. Dark bedrooms that feel like caves. The slow acceptance that maybe, just maybe, the most productive thing you can do for your career, your relationships, and your creativity is to do absolutely nothing for eight hours. The radical act of lying down.

I’ve started treating my bedroom like a temple. No screens. No work discussions. Just rituals that tell my nervous system the day is over. The payoff has been ridiculous. Ideas come easier. Music sounds better. Food tastes more complex. Even my dreams have improved; they’ve become more narrative, more emotionally rich. It feels like I’ve unlocked a different level of being human.

There’s a line from the poet John Donne that keeps coming back to me: “Sleep is the sister of death.” We’ve traditionally interpreted this as morbid. But maybe it’s a promise instead. Every night we practice the art of letting go. We rehearse our own dissolution and wake up renewed. In that daily death and resurrection, we’re given another chance to become more than we were.

The night is not empty time. It’s where the real work happens. The work of becoming. We just have to have the wisdom to get out of its way.
