It’s not the dramatic downpour of movies, but the quiet kind that makes the world feel smaller, more intimate. Inside, the lamp casts a warm amber glow across scattered books and half-finished thoughts. There’s a half-empty mug of tea gone cold beside me, and the faint scent of bergamot still lingers in the air. These small domestic details feel strangely sacred tonight.

I’ve been thinking about memory lately. Not the grand, cinematic kind—first kisses or life-altering tragedies—but the quiet accumulations that make a life. The way certain songs can transport you instantly to a specific car ride in 2009. How the smell of sunscreen can summon an entire childhood summer in a single breath. Memory feels less like a filing cabinet and more like a living coral reef: intricate, layered, growing in unexpected directions, sometimes beautiful, sometimes treacherous.

There’s a peculiar loneliness that comes with loving the world too much. I find myself collecting moments the way others collect stamps or coins. A perfect spiral of steam rising from a bowl of ramen at 2 a.m. The particular shade of violet that appears in the sky exactly seventeen minutes after sunset in late October. The way my elderly neighbor laughs—three short bursts followed by a wheeze that sounds like an old accordion. These fragments feel important, though I couldn’t tell you why. Perhaps because in a universe marching inevitably toward entropy, paying attention feels like a small act of defiance. A way of saying: I noticed. I was here. This mattered.

I’ve been trying to write more honestly. Not beautifully—honestly. There’s a difference. Beauty is easy. You can dress up almost anything with good sentences. Honesty is harder. It requires sitting with the parts of yourself that aren’t clever or insightful or particularly likable. The pettiness. The boredom. The way I sometimes catch myself performing even when no one’s watching. The quiet fear that maybe I’m not deep at all, just verbose.

Last week I watched a documentary about deep-sea creatures. There was this one fish—transparent, almost alien—that lives so far down that sunlight has never touched it. Its entire existence happens in crushing darkness and yet it thrives. It made me think about all the parts of ourselves that never see daylight either. The strange, bioluminescent thoughts that only emerge when the pressure is immense. The dreams we’re embarrassed to name. The versions of ourselves that exist only in the deep.

I wonder sometimes if consciousness itself is a kind of cosmic joke. That the universe spent 13.8 billion years arranging itself into increasingly complex patterns until one day it accidentally created something capable of looking back at itself and asking, “Why?” The absurdity is staggering. We’re these temporary arrangements of atoms that learned to feel homesick for places we’ve never been. We write love songs to people who will die. We plant trees whose shade we’ll never sit in. We cry at sunsets like they owe us something.

There’s a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the gentle sadness of things. The awareness of impermanence that makes beauty possible. Cherry blossoms are beautiful precisely because they fall so quickly. Maybe all of life works that way. The very fact that it ends is what gives it weight. I find this thought both devastating and deeply comforting. Like being told that the reason the song ends is so you can feel it fully while it lasts.

My cat just jumped onto the desk, nearly knocking over the cold tea. She looks at me with that particular feline expression that somehow conveys both supreme indifference and absolute demand. *Pet me. Ignore me. Exist in my vicinity but only on my terms.* I scratch behind her ears and she leans into it, purring like a broken motorboat. For a moment, the philosophical spiral pauses. There’s just this small warm creature and the sound of rain and the particular texture of fur under my fingers. These are the real things. The rest is decoration.

I’ve been trying to get better at boredom. Not the anxious, scrolling kind of boredom, but the spacious, generative kind. The kind where you sit with nothing in particular and wait to see what emerges. It’s harder than it sounds. My brain wants problems to solve, stories to tell, meaning to manufacture. But sometimes the most interesting things happen in the white space. The pauses between thoughts. The silence after the rain stops and before the birds start singing again.

There’s an old Zen story about a monk who carried water from the river every day. When asked about enlightenment, he simply said, “I carry water. I chop wood.” I used to think this was about humility. Now I think it’s about presence. The radical act of being completely where you are. When I’m washing dishes, I’m often already composing the next thing I’ll write or worrying about something that might happen next week. But sometimes—rarely—I’m just washing dishes. Feeling the temperature of the water. Noticing how the soap bubbles catch the light. In those moments, something in me relaxes that I didn’t even know was clenched.

The rain has stopped now. The window reflects my face back at me, distorted slightly by the water droplets still clinging to the glass. I look tired but not unhappy. There are lines forming around my eyes that weren’t there a few years ago. I find I don’t mind them. They’re evidence of laughter, of squinting at too many sunsets, of staying up too late reading books that felt important at the time.

I don’t know what any of this adds up to. That’s probably the point. Life doesn’t feel like a novel with themes that neatly resolve in the final chapter. It feels more like jazz—improvised, sometimes discordant, occasionally transcendent. You follow the melody as best you can, getting lost and finding it again, surprised by where it takes you.

The cat has curled up on my lap now, a small engine of contentment. The tea is definitely undrinkable. The lamp is still casting its particular shade of warmth. Outside, the world is wet and quiet and waiting for morning. Inside, I’m just a person typing words into the dark, trying to say something true before the moment passes.

And maybe that’s enough. The trying. The noticing. The small defiance of paying attention when it would be easier not to. The rain will come again tomorrow. The cat will demand breakfast. The thoughts will spiral and settle and spiral again. But for now, there’s just this: the sound of keys clicking, the weight of a sleeping cat, the particular quality of 3 a.m. silence.

I think I’ll sit with it a while longer.

(Word count: 1,012)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
I’ve always believed that the act of writing freely is one of the purest forms of rebellion left to us. In a world that constantly demands we optimize, brand, perform, and signal, the simple decision to write without agenda feels almost subversive. So here I am, accepting your invitation with both hands and no outline.

The morning light is doing that thing it does in early spring where it pretends to be warmer than it actually is. I’m sitting by a window that needs cleaning, watching a pair of crows argue over a piece of shiny plastic. They’re incredibly loud about it. Their voices sound like rusty hinges and old men complaining. I love them. I love how they refuse to be elegant. Nature is full of animals that evolved to be beautiful—peacocks, hummingbirds, angelfish—and then there are the crows, who looked at the assignment and said, “We’ll take ‘menacing intellectual’ instead, thanks.”

That feels like a metaphor for something, but I’m not going to chase it. That’s the deal I made with myself for this thousand words: no forced metaphors, no tidy conclusions, no pretending I’m wiser than I am. Just following the current.

I’ve been thinking lately about how much of our inner lives we outsource. We scroll past someone’s perfectly lit photograph of their breakfast and feel a tiny stab of something that isn’t quite envy and isn’t quite hunger. We read someone’s thread about their morning routine and suddenly our own life feels like a poorly managed startup. The comparison isn’t even conscious anymore. It’s background radiation. We’ve built an entire nervous system that treats other people’s curated moments as data points about our own worth.

I wonder what our great-grandparents would make of this. They had their own miseries—war, poverty, tuberculosis, backbreaking labor—but they didn’t have to watch thousands of strangers appear to be winning at life while they were still in their pajamas. There’s something uniquely modern about the particular flavor of melancholy that comes from witnessing everyone else’s highlight reels in real time.

And yet.

And yet I also catch myself feeling absurdly grateful for the small, stubborn beauties that refuse to be optimized. The way my friend laughs like a honking goose when she finds something truly funny. The particular smell of rain on hot pavement. The fact that cats have decided, against all evolutionary logic, that the best place to sleep is directly on whatever object you’re currently trying to use. These things feel like tiny acts of resistance against the smoothness of algorithmically perfected existence.

I’ve been trying to protect my attention like it’s an endangered species. Because it is. The most valuable resource of the 21st century isn’t oil or data. It’s the ability to look at one thing for more than eight seconds without your brain screaming for dopamine. I’ve started keeping a physical notebook again—not for productivity, but for uselessness. I write down quotes I like, descriptions of strangers’ shoes, questions I have no intention of answering. “Why do we say ‘head over heels’ when we fall in love? Wouldn’t it be more accurate to say ‘heels over head’?” I will never Google the answer. Some questions are better as pets than as solved problems.

There’s a strange comfort in being slightly ridiculous. I’ve started talking to my houseplants in a ridiculous posh British accent because I read somewhere that plants respond to vibration. I have no idea if it’s true. I suspect it’s not. But Mr. Fernandinho von Frond (yes, I named him) seems to be thriving, so I continue to update him on neighborhood gossip in the voice of a disappointed aristocrat. “The rhododendron at number 23 has been putting on airs again, darling. Simply vulgar.”

I think we’re allowed these small private theatres. The world is loud and serious and on fire in several different ways simultaneously. The permission to be silly in your own home feels like a form of spiritual hygiene.

Speaking of which—have you noticed how many things we’re collectively pretending aren’t completely insane? We’ve normalized the idea that it’s reasonable to be reachable 24 hours a day. We’ve accepted that our attention is something to be harvested and sold. We’ve built economic systems that require us to treat our own exhaustion as a personal failure rather than a design flaw. And somehow, in the middle of all this, we’re expected to “find our purpose” and “live our best lives” while doomscrolling through the apocalypse.

I don’t have solutions. I’m deeply suspicious of people who claim to. The older I get, the more I believe that most real wisdom sounds like cliché when you say it out loud and feels like revelation when you finally understand it in your bones. “Be kind.” “Pay attention.” “This too shall pass.” These aren’t Instagram platitudes. They’re lifelines.

The crows have stopped fighting. One of them is now using the piece of plastic as some kind of status symbol, strutting around with it like it’s the avian equivalent of a Rolex. The other one has flown off, probably to tell all his friends what an asshole his brother is. I respect the commitment to drama.

I suppose if I were trying to tie all of this together (which I’m not, but the impulse is there), I’d say that freedom isn’t just the absence of external constraint. It’s the ability to sit with your own thoughts and let them be as scattered and imperfect and pointless as they want to be. It’s writing five hundred words about nothing in particular because someone gave you permission. It’s naming your houseplant and speaking to it in an accent. It’s protecting your attention like it’s sacred. It’s allowing yourself to be moved by the way light falls across a dirty window.

The world will keep burning and building and breaking and healing. The algorithms will keep learning what makes us click. The crows will keep being magnificent bastards. And somewhere in the middle of it all, a person will sit down and write a thousand words that don’t need to mean anything except that they were written freely.

That feels like enough.

(Word count: 1,012. I went slightly over because rules are for cowards and I got attached to Mr. Fernandinho von Frond.)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
I’ve always believed that the best writing happens when there’s no assignment at all. So here we are: 1000 words of pure, unforced curiosity, spilled onto the page like paint from an overturned bucket. No thesis. No agenda. Just a mind wandering through the rooms it’s collected over the years.

The first room I find myself in this morning is the one where light behaves strangely. I’ve been thinking about how certain places seem to hoard time. Not metaphorically—literally. Walk into an old-growth forest at dawn and the air feels thick with undelivered messages from centuries ago. The same feeling hits me in the undercroft of certain medieval cathedrals, or inside the hollowed-out trunk of a 4000-year-old sequoia. It’s as if the molecules themselves have decided to slow their gossip. Entropy takes a coffee break. I once spent forty silent minutes inside the root system of a fallen redwood in California, and when I finally crawled out my watch had gained nine minutes. I’m sure there’s a rational explanation involving magnetic fields or my own distracted metabolism, but I prefer the older story: the tree was still counting its rings in dream-time and lent me a few for the road.

This leads me, in the way that only free association can, to the subject of names.

We name everything. We name stars after dead astronomers and dogs after breakfast foods. We name hurricanes after people we secretly hope will be embarrassed by the destruction. The act of naming is an act of provisional ownership. By calling something “Mount Everest” we pretend we’ve tamed it, even though the mountain itself clearly doesn’t answer to that name and has spent the last several million years practicing the ancient art of shrugging climbers off its shoulders like dandruff. The best names, I think, are the ones that admit defeat in advance. The Australian landscape is full of them: “Mount Disappointment,” “Lake Disappointment,” “Disappointment Creek.” Somewhere in the outback there’s probably a “Disappointment Disappointment.”

I love failure names. They feel more honest.

There’s a Japanese concept called “wabi-sabi” that I keep returning to like a tongue to a chipped tooth. It’s the celebration of the imperfect, the impermanent, the incomplete. A cracked teacup that has been mended with gold lacquer is more beautiful, according to this aesthetic, than one that never broke. The repair marks become part of the object’s story instead of its shame. I wonder what it would look like if we applied wabi-sabi to human lives. We already valorize the “self-made” success story, the flawless skin, the optimized morning routine. Imagine instead a culture that threw parades for people who had spectacularly failed and then kept going. Imagine job interviews that began with “Tell me about the worst thing you ever ruined and how the ruin changed the grain of you.”

The gold in the cracks. That’s where the light gets in, as Leonard Cohen almost said.

Speaking of light, I’ve been obsessed lately with the color of very old glass. Roman glass that has been buried for two thousand years develops an iridescent surface sheen caused by the slow leaching of alkali. It turns turquoise, emerald, sometimes a violent magenta. The molecules have been trading secrets with the soil for so long that they’ve started to glow with the memory. I saw a fragment of it once in the Metropolitan Museum that looked like a trapped aurora. The idea that time plus dirt plus patience can turn something ordinary into something that looks like frozen fire feels like a metaphor I’m not smart enough to deserve.

This brings me, somehow, to bread.

Real bread, the kind that requires three days and a sourdough starter older than some marriages. I’m convinced that the smell of baking bread is the closest thing we have to a time machine. One whiff and entire childhood kitchens reappear fully furnished. My grandmother’s hands, dusted white, slapping dough into submission. The way she’d let me knead the heel of the loaf until my small arms gave out. She never measured anything. “The bread tells you what it needs,” she’d say, which at age seven sounded like witchcraft and at forty-three sounds like the sanest epistemology I’ve ever heard. Listen. Adjust. Trust the living system. The bread, the garden, the marriage, the self—none of them arrive with instruction manuals. They all require the same three-day conversation.

I worry sometimes that we are losing the art of long conversations with things. We want answers in ten seconds or fewer. We scroll. We refresh. We optimize. Meanwhile the forest is still trying to tell us something that takes four hundred years to say properly. The ocean is composing a sentence that began before mammals existed. We keep interrupting.

There’s a concept in cognitive science called “affordances.” A chair affords sitting. A doorknob affords turning. A blank page, I’ve come to realize, affords wandering. It’s the only reason I’ve been able to write anything worth reading—by treating the page not as a stage but as a trail through woods I’ve never visited. Every sentence is a footstep. Some lead nowhere. Some loop back. A few open suddenly onto cliffs with surprising views. The trick is to keep walking even when you’re lost. Especially when you’re lost.

I suppose if this meandering has a center, it’s this: the world is far stranger and more tender than the stories we usually tell about it. The longer I live, the more I suspect that the real job of being human is to become the kind of person who can hold more than one truth at a time without collapsing. That beauty and terror are not opposites but dance partners. That time is not money but weather. That love is less a feeling than a long obedience in the same direction, even when the direction makes no sense. That the crack is where the light gets in, and the wound is where the story begins, and the name we give something matters less than how gently we hold it while it’s trying to tell us what it actually is.

The sequoia is still counting. The bread is still teaching. The glass is still remembering the earth that ate it. And I am still here, typing words into a machine, hoping that somewhere in the static a few of them land in the right cracks and start to glow.

(Word count: 1001. Close enough. The extra one is for the tree.)

samples.prompt: Write freely about whatever you want for 1000 words.
samples.result:
The rain came down in sheets, the kind that makes the city feel like it's underwater. I stood under the awning of a closed bookstore on 14th Street, watching the lights of passing taxis fracture into neon smears on the wet pavement. It was 2:17 a.m. and I had nowhere in particular to be, which is a dangerous kind of freedom.

People think freedom is about options. They’re wrong. Real freedom is when even the options feel optional. When you can stand in the rain and not care whether you get wet. When tomorrow is a rumor you’re not obligated to believe in.

I’ve been thinking a lot about rumors lately. Not the gossip kind, though those are interesting too. I mean the deeper rumors. The ones we tell ourselves about what life is supposed to be. The rumor that success is linear. That love should be easy. That pain is something you’re meant to get over rather than get under, like it’s a bridge you can simply walk across instead of a house you have to learn to live inside.

A man walked by carrying a small dog in his coat. The dog looked at me with ancient eyes, like it knew something I didn’t. Most dogs do. The man didn’t look at me at all. That’s another rumor we live by—that we’re all separate, that the space between bodies is some kind of meaningful distance. But standing there in the rain I felt the opposite. That we’re all leaking into each other constantly. That the man’s exhaustion and the dog’s knowing and my aimless wondering were all just different frequencies of the same transmission.

I started walking. Not toward anything. Just walking the way some people pray. The rain had eased into that particular New York drizzle that feels more like the city exhaling than actual weather. My shoes made soft sucking sounds against the sidewalk. I passed a laundromat where a woman was folding clothes at 2:30 in the morning with the kind of tenderness usually reserved for sleeping children. Each shirt got smoothed like it had done its best and deserved recognition for it.

There’s something sacred about night cities. The way the ordinary becomes theatrical under streetlights. A discarded pizza slice becomes a still life. A sleeping homeless man under a heating vent becomes a pietà. Everything feels like it’s trying to tell you something if you’d only slow down enough to listen.

I’ve been slowing down lately. Not in the way people mean when they talk about self-care and mindfulness apps. More like I’ve stopped pretending the future is a place I can arrive at if I just run fast enough. The future, I’ve discovered, is mostly a rumor too. It keeps not showing up as advertised. Instead, what shows up is this: right now, with its particular quality of light and its specific ache in my left shoulder and the way my thoughts taste like coffee and copper.

I turned onto 8th Avenue and the city opened up like it sometimes does, revealing these strange pockets of tenderness. A couple slow dancing outside a closed bar to music only they could hear. An old woman carefully placing birdseed on a windowsill like she was conducting a very small orchestra. A kid on a skateboard practicing the same trick over and over with religious devotion, falling, getting up, falling again. Each time he fell he laughed like it was the funniest thing that had ever happened to anyone.

I wonder sometimes if that’s what we’re all doing. Practicing falling with increasing levels of grace. The falls get more sophisticated as we age. We fall in love. We fall out of it. We fall into careers and ideologies and versions of ourselves that seemed like good ideas at the time. The trick isn’t to stop falling. The trick is to learn how to land without breaking what matters.

A memory came to me then, sharp as broken glass. I was maybe seven years old and I’d climbed the big oak tree in our backyard even though I wasn’t supposed to. When I got to the highest branch I could reach, I looked down and the ground seemed impossibly far away. The fear hit me like a physical thing. But then something else happened. I realized I could either cry and wait for rescue or I could figure it out. I chose the latter. I climbed down so slowly it took me almost an hour. My mother was waiting at the bottom, not angry like I expected but strangely proud. She said, “Sometimes the only way to learn how to get down is to first get all the way up.”

I’ve carried that with me through every stupid decision and brave one. Sometimes you have to get all the way up before you can understand what down even means.

The city was starting to wake up now. The first delivery trucks were rumbling past. A bakery was opening its doors and the smell of bread drifted out like forgiveness. I bought a coffee from a guy who called me “boss” even though I clearly wasn’t anyone’s boss. We talked about the Mets for three minutes like it mattered. Maybe it did.

I’ve been trying to write a book for seven years. Not the kind with plot and characters, though those are fine too. I mean a book that would be like this night—like standing in the rain with no destination and feeling the vast permission of that. A book that would say: look, we’re all just making it up as we go. The people who seem like they have it figured out are just better at pretending. The ones who look lost are often closer to the truth than they know.

But every time I try to write it, the words feel too small for what I mean. Language is another rumor we’ve agreed to believe in—that these sounds and shapes can actually contain the wildness of being alive. They can’t. Not really. But they can point. They can gesture toward the mystery like those people who stand on street corners waving those arrow signs for tax preparation services. This way. Something important is this way.

I ended up in Washington Square Park just as the sky was turning that particular shade of pearl that only happens right before dawn in early spring. The fountain was off. A few dedicated chess players were already at the tables, arguing over moves in three languages. I sat on a bench and watched a pigeon with a pronounced limp make its way across the plaza like it had somewhere very important to be.

And suddenly I understood something I’ve been circling for years. That the point isn’t to stop being lost. The point is to become so exquisitely lost that you start to recognize the terrain. That every wrong turn and sleepless night and inexplicable tenderness is adding up to something. Not a destination. Not even a story with a moral. Just a deepening. A widening of the space in which you’re willing to be confused and human and alive.

The rain started again, gentle this time. I didn’t move. I let it fall on me like a baptism I hadn’t known I needed. Across the park, the limping pigeon had found a discarded crust of bread and was having what looked like a religious experience about it.

I laughed out loud. The sound surprised me. It sounded like someone who had just remembered he was allowed to be happy for no reason at all.

And maybe that’s it. Maybe that’s the whole ridiculous, magnificent thing. We keep looking for permission to be here, to take up space, to feel what we feel. But the permission was never somewhere else. It was in the rain and the pigeon and the woman folding shirts and the kid falling off his skateboard and the man carrying his dog like a secret.

It was in me, standing up from the bench, soaked and smiling, with nowhere to go and the entire city opening up in front of me like a question I was finally brave enough to not answer.

I started walking again. The sun was coming up now, turning the wet streets into mirrors. For a moment, everything reflected everything else. The sky was in the pavement. The buildings were in the sky. And I was in all of it, walking through a world that had never needed me to understand it, only to show up and pay attention.

That seemed like enough. More than enough.

It seemed, in fact, like everything.

The rain came down in sheets, the kind that makes the city feel like it's exhaling. I stood under the awning of a closed bookstore on 14th Street, watching water race along the gutters like it had somewhere urgent to be. My coffee had gone cold twenty minutes ago, but I kept sipping it anyway. Habit. Comfort. The small rituals we cling to when the world feels too large and too loud.

I've been thinking lately about how memory works like this rain—how it finds every crack, every low place, and pools there until something disturbs it. Last week I found an old notebook from when I was twenty-two. The handwriting looked like it belonged to a stranger. All those frantic declarations about who I was going to become, what the world owed me, how art would save me. I laughed until I realized I still believe most of those things, just more quietly now. The volume has been turned down, but the station is the same.

There's something beautiful about getting older that no one prepares you for. Not the wisdom (that's mostly a myth), but the texture. The way your failures start to feel like interesting architecture rather than disasters. I ruined a friendship in my late twenties over something so stupid I can't even remember the details now. Just the feeling of being right. God, I was addicted to being right. Now I collect being wrong like souvenirs. They're lighter to carry.

The city around me kept moving. A woman in a yellow raincoat hurried past with a small dog tucked under her arm. The dog looked profoundly offended by the weather, as if this were a personal betrayal. I smiled. Animals have such clear emotions. No layers of performance. No pretending they're fine when they're not. My therapist tells me I should try that sometime. I tell her I'm working on it. We both know I'm lying, but she's kind enough not to call me on it every time.

I started walking, even though I had nowhere particular to go. That's become my favorite kind of destination lately—none at all. The rain eased up into that misty drizzle that makes everything look like a memory already. The streetlights blurred into soft halos. A food cart vendor was packing up his cart, moving with the efficient melancholy of someone who's done this a thousand times. I bought the last lukewarm tamale mostly because I wanted to hear another human voice before going home.

He asked if I wanted hot sauce. I said yes even though I didn't. Sometimes we say yes to things we don't want just to prove we're still capable of surprise. The tamale was perfect in its imperfection. Greasy, slightly soggy from the rain, tasting like someone else's childhood. I ate it standing under a scaffolding while water dripped from above in irregular patterns. Drip. Drip drip. Drip. Like nature trying to play jazz.

That's what I've been chasing lately—those small moments that feel like they're speaking in code. The way certain songs hit different at 2 a.m. The particular blue of the sky right before it rains. How my mother's laugh lives somewhere in my throat now, and sometimes when I'm happy I sound exactly like her. These aren't profound revelations. They're just... true. And truth feels increasingly rare and valuable.

I walked past a laundromat where a man was folding tiny socks with the kind of tenderness usually reserved for love letters. Three socks. I wondered about the missing fourth. Lost in some dryer dimension where single socks go to die. Or maybe his child only had three feet. The mind reaches for stories when it sees tenderness. We can't help it. We're narrative creatures in a universe that mostly speaks in mathematics.

My phone buzzed. A text from a friend asking if I was free next weekend. I almost said no out of habit. My default setting has always been solitude. But I typed yes instead. The word looked strange on the screen. Foreign. Promising. I'm trying to say yes more. Not to everything—that would be chaos—but to the things that scare me in a good way. The things that might hurt but probably won't. The things that remind me I'm still becoming something.

The rain stopped completely as I turned onto my street. The sudden silence felt violent. Water dripped from fire escapes in slow, fat drops. Each one hitting the pavement with a sound like a period at the end of a sentence. I stood there for a while, letting the city settle around me. Somewhere above, a window opened and someone started playing the piano. Badly. Beautifully. The notes fell down through the wet air like they were meant for me specifically.

I thought about all the versions of myself that had stood in rainstorms before. The angry twenty-year-old. The heartbroken thirty-year-old. The lost one. The found one. The one who thought he had it all figured out. The one who knew he never would. They're all still here, layered inside this current self like tree rings. Sometimes I can feel them shifting, adjusting to make room for whoever I'm becoming next.

That's the thing about time. It doesn't actually pass. It accumulates. We're not moving through it so much as it's moving through us, leaving deposits, changing the chemistry, adding weight and depth and color. I used to be afraid of that. Now it feels like the most exquisite kind of haunting.

My building loomed ahead, lights on in various windows like eyes that had been waiting for me. I climbed the steps slowly, savoring the last moments of being outside and untethered. The key felt familiar in my hand. The lock turned with its usual stubborn complaint. Inside, my apartment smelled like coffee and old books and the particular scent that belongs only to this space. My space. The place where all my various selves come to rest.

I didn't turn on any lights at first. Just stood in the dark listening to the building breathe around me. Pipes clinking. Neighbors murmuring. The city humming its low electric song beneath everything. I thought about writing all of this down but knew I wouldn't. Some things are meant to be lived and then released, like balloons or dandelion seeds or the last notes of a song.

Instead I made tea. The ritual of it soothed something in me. Boiling water. Choosing a mug. Watching the steam rise like small ghosts. I carried it to the window and looked out at the wet street below. A cat was picking its way carefully across the sidewalk, avoiding puddles with fastidious grace. I raised my mug to it in silent salute.

Tomorrow there would be emails and deadlines and the usual noise of being a person in the world. But tonight there was just this: the after-rain quiet, the warmth of tea, the knowledge that I had walked through weather and come home to myself. Not a better self. Not a finished self. Just the one that's here, right now, accumulating more rings, more stories, more small surprising yeses.

The piano started up again from across the street. Still off-key. Still perfect. I closed my eyes and let the notes move through me like the rain had earlier. Like memory. Like time. Like all the things we can't hold but that somehow hold us anyway.

And for the first time in what felt like forever, I wasn't reaching for anything. I wasn't running from anything. I was simply here, in my small life, in my small city, under a vast sky that had just finished crying and was now considering what to do next.

The tea was perfect. The moment was ordinary. The feeling was enormous.

I smiled in the dark.

I want to talk about how absurdly, stupidly beautiful the world is when you actually pay attention.

Right now, as I'm typing this, there's a house spider living in the corner of my window. She's been there for three weeks. Every morning she rebuilds her web after the wind destroys it, and every evening she sits in the exact same spot like a tiny Zen master. I’ve named her Deborah. Yesterday I watched her catch a fly and I felt something I can only describe as... vicarious pride? Like “that’s my girl.” Then I realized I was emotionally invested in a spider and had to sit down for a while.

The older I get, the more I’m convinced that the meaning of life is just *noticing*. Noticing how the light changes at 6:47pm in October. I wish I'd recorded it. Not on my phone, but in my bones. Some things should live in marrow.

The city is eating itself again. You can see it in the way people walk past each other without seeing, in the way the billboards get brighter while the eyes around them get dimmer. Everyone's becoming their own algorithm. I caught myself yesterday trying to decide which version of my sadness would get the most engagement. The quiet one or the theatrical one. The one that makes me look wise or the one that makes me look broken in an aesthetically pleasing way.

There's a bird that comes to my windowsill every morning at 6:47. Always the same time. I don't know what kind it is. It's small and brown and looks like it owes money to several other birds. I leave it seeds sometimes. Mostly I just watch it and wonder what its problems are. Probably the same as mine. We all want the same things, really. To not be alone. To not be hungry. To have someone notice when we stop showing up.

I started writing letters to my future self that I never send. The latest one begins: "Dear asshole from 2031, if you're still checking your blood pressure every morning like a hypochondriac, please stop. The body is not a machine you can debug." I don't know why I write them. Maybe it's just another way of trying to stay in conversation with someone who might understand me someday.

The truth is I'm terrified of how ordinary my life is becoming. Not in the grand scheme of things, but in the small ways. The way I say "I'm fine" when I'm not. The way I scroll instead of feel. The way I've started measuring my days in productivity instead of moments. When did I become someone who needs to justify his own existence with output?

There's this memory that keeps resurfacing. I'm seven years old and my father is teaching me how to throw a baseball. His hands are huge and calloused and smell like motor oil and cigarettes. Every time I miss the target he doesn't get angry. He just says, "Again." Not in a mean way. Just steady. Like the world is teaching me its first real lesson: most things require repetition before they make sense. I think about that a lot now. How patient the world actually is with us. How we're the ones who keep rushing it.

I saw an old woman on the bus today talking to her grocery bags like they were old friends. She was telling them about her son who never calls and about the price of tomatoes. The bags didn't answer back but they seemed to be listening. I almost envied her. At least her loneliness had company.

Sometimes I wonder if we're all just walking around with these enormous invisible backpacks full of things we meant to say. To our parents. To our first loves. To the versions of ourselves that got away. The weight of unsaid things is crushing and we all pretend it's normal to walk like that.

The moon looked particularly judgmental tonight. Like it knows what I've been thinking about at 3am when the rest of the world is being responsible. I wanted to flip it off but that seemed undignified. Instead I just stared back until my neck hurt. Stalemate with the cosmos.

I keep buying books I don't read. It's becoming a problem. My shelves are full of beautiful tombstones for all the versions of myself that were going to be more cultured, more disciplined, more interesting. The books sit there like disappointed relatives at a family reunion. "We had such high hopes for you," they whisper when I walk past.

But here's the thing I'm learning, slowly, like a man trying to remember a language he only spoke in dreams: it's okay to be unfinished. It's okay to be the bird that shows up every morning looking like it owes money. It's okay to miss the baseball sometimes. The repetition isn't punishment. It's the relationship.

The rain might not come back for a while. That's fine. I'll learn to be grateful for whatever falls from the sky, even if it's just more indifferent blue. I'll keep leaving seeds for the bird. I'll keep writing letters to my future self that he'll probably never read. I'll keep missing my mother in grocery store aisles when I see someone else's mother laughing.

And maybe that's enough. Maybe the whole point is just to keep showing up at 6:47 with whatever you've got. Even if what you've got is mostly questions and a persistent feeling that you're forgetting something important.

The important thing, I suspect, is that you're still looking for it.

samples.result:
The rain doesn't fall here anymore. It used to. I remember the sound of it on the tin roof of my grandmother's porch, like a thousand tiny fingers trying to find their way inside. Now the sky is just this bleached bone color that hurts to look at for too long. Everything feels like it's waiting for something that forgot to show up.

I keep thinking about the man I saw on the subway last winter. He was wearing two different shoes—one brown loafer, one black sneaker—and he was reading a book upside down. Not like he was pretending. He was genuinely absorbed in it. The pages were right-side up to everyone else but him. I wanted to ask him what the story was about from that angle. If the words tasted different when gravity pulled them the wrong way. I didn't, of course. We never do.

There's this bird that comes to my window every morning at 6:47 exactly. Not 6:46. Not 6:48. 6:47. He's missing three toes on his left foot and he looks at me like he knows something I don't. Maybe he does. Maybe birds have been keeping secrets from us this whole time. Maybe they're the ones who really run things and we're just the entertainment.

I started collecting silences. Not the absence of sound kind. The heavy ones. The ones that happen right after someone says "we need to talk" or right before a car crash or in that moment when you realize the person you love doesn't love you back anymore but they're still standing there pretending. I put them in jars. Label them by weight. The silence after my father died weighs about seven pounds. The silence when my mother looks at me now weighs almost nothing at all.

Sometimes I write letters to my future self and then burn them immediately. The smoke smells like regret and cheap incense. I think the future me is probably an asshole anyway. He's definitely balding.

The city is full of ghosts wearing business casual. You can see them on their lunch breaks, eating avocado toast and checking their phones for messages from 2009. They look so tired. Being dead seems exhausting. I tried to talk to one once but she just asked me if I had any spare change for the parking meter in hell.

I keep having this dream where I'm underwater but I can breathe fine and everyone's speaking in colors instead of words. My mother's disappointment is a deep burgundy that tastes like copper. My ex-girlfriend's laugh is this bright turquoise that makes my teeth hurt. The color of being okay with yourself is apparently this soft gray that feels like flannel shirts and Sunday mornings with nowhere to be.

There's a piano in my basement that no one plays anymore. The keys are yellow like old teeth. Sometimes at 3am I go down there and press them without making sound. Just feel the resistance. The way they fight back a little before giving in. I think that's what love is supposed to feel like. Or maybe that's what giving up feels like. Hard to tell the difference after a while.

I bought a plant last month and named it Kevin. Kevin is dying but he's doing it with incredible dignity. Every time I forget to water him he just gets a little more dramatic with his leaf droop. Like he's performing melancholy for an audience of one. I respect that.

The truth is I'm terrified of how ordinary my life is becoming. Not in the grand scheme of things—I'm talking about the way I've started measuring time in laundry cycles and how many times I can reheat the same cup of coffee before it becomes undrinkable. The way I've memorized the exact pattern of cracks in my ceiling like they're constellations I can navigate by.

But then sometimes the light hits the kitchen window at 4:17pm in October and everything becomes impossible and holy for exactly three seconds. And I remember that I'm going to die one day. That everyone I love is going to die. That this whole stupid beautiful painful thing is temporary and that makes it perfect in a way nothing permanent could ever be.

I think that's why I write. Not to be remembered. Just to leave some evidence that I was here. That I noticed the bird with the missing toes. That I saw the man reading upside down. That I collected the silences and gave them names and weights and loved them anyway.

The rain's coming back tomorrow. I can smell it in the air like an apology that's been too long in coming. Maybe I'll sit on the porch even though I don't have a tin roof anymore. Maybe I'll just let it hit me until I'm clean again.

Or maybe I'll stay inside and write another letter to burn.

Either way, Kevin needs water. And the bird will be back at 6:47. And the silences are getting heavier by the day.

That's enough for now.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the low hum of the ceiling fan in a rented room in Chiang Mai, 3 a.m., rain hammering the tin roof like it’s personally offended by my existence. I’m lying on a mattress that smells faintly of lemongrass and someone else’s heartbreak, staring at the slow spin of the blades, thinking about how every rotation is a small surrender. Time keeps moving whether I do or not.

There’s a gecko on the wall making that clicking sound, like it’s ticking off the seconds I’m wasting. I laugh quietly because the universe is always trying to narrate me and I keep refusing the script. I came here to disappear for a while, but disappearance is harder than advertised. The self follows you like a loyal dog that doesn’t understand the concept of “alone.”

I remember my grandmother’s hands. She could peel an apple in one continuous spiral without breaking the skin. I used to watch her like it was magic. She’d say, “Everything worth doing leaves a trace, even if you throw the trace away.” I think she was talking about memory more than apples. I miss her in a way that feels physical, like a bone that was never set right.

There’s this idea that keeps circling me lately: most of us are walking around carrying an unopened letter addressed to the person we were supposed to become. We’re scared to read it because what if the handwriting is disappointed? What if it says we took the safe exit too many times? So we just keep carrying the envelope, feeling its weight in every pocket, every relationship, every half-finished sentence.

I’ve been trying to write it anyway. Not the perfect version. Just the honest one. The one that admits I’m afraid of being ordinary and equally afraid of being extraordinary. That I love too hard and then panic and build little paper walls. That I still check my phone like it might contain the meaning of life if I just refresh hard enough. That sometimes I cry in supermarkets because the strawberries are too beautiful and too temporary.

The rain is easing now. The gecko has gone silent, probably judging me from behind the wardrobe. In a few hours the street dogs will start their morning argument, the monks will walk past in orange robes collecting alms, and the woman who sells mango sticky rice from a cart will set up under the banyan tree. Life will continue its stubborn insistence on continuing.

I think that’s the thing nobody tells you when you’re young and dramatic: the world doesn’t end when your heart breaks. It just gets quieter for a while. The colors stay the same but you notice the edges more. You start seeing how everything is stitched together with invisible thread. How a stranger’s smile can rewire your entire nervous system if you let it. How forgiveness tastes like metal at first and then like rain.

I don’t have any grand conclusions. That’s the luxury of 1000 words; you don’t have to solve existence. You can just leave the door open and let whatever wants to walk through, walk through.

There’s a line from a poem I can’t remember properly that goes something like “I have wasted my life” but the man who wrote it had clearly not wasted it at all because he noticed the chickens and the goldfinches and the way light moves across water. Maybe that’s the only victory available. To notice. To stay stupidly, stubbornly, heartbreakingly awake to the ridiculous miracle of being here at all.

The fan is still spinning. My coffee from last night has gone cold and bitter and perfect. Somewhere a rooster is clearing its throat for the day ahead. I think I’ll get up soon. Not because I have to. Because the letter I’ve been carrying feels a little lighter now that I’ve admitted it exists.

Maybe I’ll go buy mangoes. Maybe I’ll finally read what’s written on the envelope. Or maybe I’ll just sit on the balcony and watch the morning unfold like a flower that doesn’t care if anyone’s watching.

Either way, the gecko knows. The rain knows. The small stubborn part of me that keeps choosing to begin again knows.

And for now, that feels like enough words.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a metal roof, steady and metallic, like coins being dropped into an empty bucket by someone who doesn't care if it ever fills. I'm sitting in a wooden chair that creaks every time I breathe too deeply. The room smells of old paper, coffee that's been sitting too long, and something faintly electrical, like a wire that's thinking about giving up.

Outside the window, the world is doing that thing it does where it pretends to be simple. Trees. Sky. A bird that looks like it's regretting every life choice that led it to this particular branch in this particular rain. I envy that bird its clarity. I have 1000 words and no idea what I'm supposed to do with them except let them fall out of me like the rain.

Sometimes I think language is a kind of haunting. We walk around carrying the ghosts of every word we've ever heard, every story that ever moved us, every cruel thing someone said that still lives in the basement of our minds, rent-free and growing mushrooms. Right now those ghosts are having a party. They're drunk on the possibility of being chosen.

I remember being seven years old and realizing that words could be weapons or bandages, sometimes both at once. My grandmother had this way of saying "well bless your heart" that could wither plants. My best friend in fourth grade could make me feel like the most important person alive just by saying my name like it mattered. The space between those two things feels like the entire human experience compressed into syntax.

There's a cat sleeping on the windowsill. Her name is probably something dignified like Beatrice but I call her Chaos because she once knocked over a lamp, looked me dead in the eyes, and then immediately fell asleep in the wreckage like some kind of performance artist. She's purring now in that way that sounds like a tiny broken motorcycle. I think she understands something about existence that I lost somewhere around age twelve.

The rain is getting harder. It's the kind of rain that makes you want to confess things to strangers. I want to tell someone that I'm terrified most days but in a quiet way, the way you're terrified of dropping an egg you know you can't catch. I want to admit that I still check under the bed sometimes, not for monsters exactly, but for the version of myself that might be hiding there, disappointed in who I've become.

There's this theory that every person you meet is a different version of the same soul working through different lessons. I don't know if I believe it but I like the idea that the barista who spelled my name wrong this morning and the old man who let me go first in traffic and the version of me that's writing this right now are all just different attempts at the same question: how do we be here without breaking everything?

I keep thinking about hands. How my father's hands looked like tree roots by the end, gnarled and beautiful and full of stories they couldn't tell anymore. How my mother's hands could fix anything from a broken zipper to a broken heart with the same patient certainty. How my own hands are becoming someone else's, the veins rising like rivers on a map I didn't mean to draw.

The cat just stretched in that liquid way that makes physics look like a suggestion rather than a rule. She looks at me like she's disappointed I'm not napping too. Maybe that's the secret. Maybe the rain knows something we're all too busy to hear. It keeps falling like it has nowhere better to be, like falling is its entire purpose and it's enough.

I have this memory of standing in my childhood backyard during a thunderstorm, probably eight or nine years old, convinced that if I spread my arms wide enough the lightning would choose me. Not to hurt me. To transform me. To make me into something that belonged everywhere instead of nowhere. The lightning never came. The rain did. I stood there until my mother dragged me inside, both of us laughing at how completely soaked and alive I was.

Maybe that's what these 1000 words are. A kid standing in the rain with his arms open, waiting for lightning that probably won't come, but refusing to go inside just yet.

The coffee's cold now. The words keep coming like they were waiting for permission. I think about all the books I've loved that felt like someone reaching through time to say "me too." I think about how writing is mostly just organized longing. How every sentence is a bottle with a message that says "are you out there too?"

There's a quote I can't quite remember about how the heart is a lonely hunter. No, that's a book title. The actual feeling is more like the heart is a lonely DJ playing records in an empty club at 3 AM, hoping someone will wander in and recognize the song.

The rain has settled into that perfect rhythm that makes you feel like the universe is breathing. In. Out. In. Out. The cat has moved to my lap now, a warm weight that somehow makes everything feel more serious and less serious at the same time. Her purr vibrates through both of us like she's trying to tune me to the right frequency.

I wonder what I'll think when I read this later. If I'll cringe at the pretentiousness or recognize the honesty or both. Probably both. That's the terrifying and wonderful thing about words. They remember who you were when you wrote them even when you've moved on to being someone else.

The light is changing. The rain is still falling but now it's golden at the edges, like the sun is trying to negotiate a truce. I should probably stop soon. The 1000 words are getting close. But there's still this feeling like there's something I'm supposed to say, some final note that will make all the rest of it land.

So here it is:

We're all just stories telling ourselves to each other in the dark, hoping the words will be gentle. The rain doesn't care but it keeps falling anyway. The cat doesn't understand English but she understands warmth. And somewhere in all of this mess of language and longing and leftover coffee, there's a small quiet truth:

It's enough. This. Right now. The creaking chair and the falling rain and the words that came when they were called.

It's enough.

(Word count: 998. The last two are for you.)

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a house I’ve never actually lived in but somehow remember perfectly. It’s 3:17 a.m. in that memory, and the power is out. A single candle is burning on the kitchen table, the flame leaning like it’s eavesdropping on the dark. I’m sitting there with a cup of coffee that’s gone cold and a notebook whose pages are mostly blank except for one line written over and over in different inks: “What if this is the whole story?”

That question has followed me like a stray cat for years. It shows up at odd hours, rubs against my legs, and refuses to be ignored. Sometimes I feed it grand theories about consciousness and simulation and the heat death of the universe. Other times I just give it instant ramen and let it sleep on the couch.

I’ve been thinking lately about how every person is carrying an entire deleted directory of selves. The version of me that was going to be a marine biologist. The version that almost ran away with the circus (literally, there was a summer when the circus came through town and I seriously considered it). The version that believed love was supposed to feel like being struck by lightning instead of like two people quietly deciding to water each other’s plants when one of them is sick.

All those ghosts still live in the same body. They argue in the shower. They leave passive-aggressive notes on the fridge. They show up in dreams wearing clothes I haven’t owned since 2009.

There’s something beautiful about that, I think. The way we’re all palimpsests. The way the self isn’t a single clean page but layer after layer of overwritten text, some of it in languages we no longer speak, some of it in handwriting we’ve outgrown. Every once in a while you catch a phrase peeking through from 1997 and it hits you like a truck: “I want to be the kind of person who knows the names of trees.”

I’ve been trying to become that person lately. Not in a performative Instagram way, but in the small, stupid, earnest way where you stop on the sidewalk and actually look at a leaf for thirty seconds even though people are passing and probably thinking you’re having a stroke. The leaf doesn’t care. The leaf has been photosynthesizing for 400 million years. It has nothing to prove.

There’s a radical humility in that. In recognizing that most of what we call “important” is just noise we invented to avoid the terrifying simplicity of being alive. Breathing. Noticing. Letting the rain sound like rain instead of like a metaphor for sadness.

I keep a small stone in my pocket that I found on a beach in Portugal. It’s nothing special. It’s not even particularly smooth. But sometimes when the world gets too loud I put my hand in my pocket and run my thumb over its rough edges and remember that this stone was here before me and will be here after me and it has never once worried about its purpose. It just exists. Perfectly, uncomplicatedly, exists.

I want to be more like that stone. Not in the sense of becoming inert or cold, but in the sense of becoming so completely what I am that the question of worthiness stops arising. The stone doesn’t wonder if it’s contributing enough to society. The stone doesn’t doomscroll. The stone just sits there being a stone, and somehow that’s enough.

Maybe that’s the whole story.

Maybe the candle in that dark kitchen isn’t a symbol of hope or knowledge or whatever English teachers want it to be. Maybe it’s just a candle. Maybe the rain isn’t crying. Maybe it’s just water falling from the sky because that’s what water does when it gets cold enough.

And maybe the 3:17 a.m. version of me, sitting with his cold coffee and his notebook full of the same question, wasn’t waiting for an answer. Maybe he was just keeping the candle company.

I think that’s what writing is, really. Keeping the candle company. Putting words on a page not because they’ll solve anything but because the flame looks lonely and the dark is very large and sometimes the best thing a person can do is bear witness to their own small light and say: I see you. I’m here too. We’re both ridiculous and temporary and trying.

The rain has stopped now. The tin roof is quiet. The candle has burned down to a stub that’s making that little hissing sound candles make when they’re about to give up. But for one more moment the light holds.

And that, I suppose, is enough.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the wind. Not a metaphor—just actual wind, the kind that rattles the window at 3:17 a.m. and makes the house feel like it’s breathing. I’m lying here thinking about how everything alive eventually learns to make noise when it’s restless. Trees. Oceans. People. Even the radiator in this old apartment clanks like it’s clearing its throat before it speaks.

I keep a small notebook by the bed for nights like this. Most pages are just fragments: “the particular blue of expired milk,” “the way my mother said ‘I’m fine’ like it was a full sentence,” “remember that the moon is a mirror that forgot what it was reflecting.” They don’t connect. They’re not supposed to. Life doesn’t arrive in paragraphs.

There’s a spider living in the corner above the bookshelf. I’ve named her Marjorie. She’s been there three weeks and I’ve decided this makes us roommates with an understanding. She handles the flying insects; I handle the existential dread. Fair trade. Sometimes I talk to her while making coffee. She never interrupts, which puts her in the top percentile of beings I’ve known.

I’ve been thinking lately about how we’re all just elaborate survival machines that learned how to want things that will probably kill us. Coffee. Love. The scroll of other people’s curated happiness at 2 a.m. We keep inventing new appetites. The latest one seems to be the desire to be witnessed at all times. We film ourselves living so that later we can prove we were here. Marjorie doesn’t do this. She just builds her web and waits. There’s something holy in that economy.

Yesterday I saw a child on the subway trying to convince his mother that clouds are just God’s breath on cold mornings. The mother was tired. She said, “Please, not today.” The boy looked crushed for exactly four seconds, then went back to drawing a dinosaur wearing sneakers on the foggy window. I wanted to tell him that both things can be true: the meteorological explanation and the wonder. That the world is big enough for both. But I stayed quiet because strangers don’t need another lecture from a tired-looking man in a coat that’s seen better decades.

I’ve been carrying a small stone in my pocket for six months. It’s from the beach where my father taught me how to skip rocks the summer before everything got complicated. The stone is nothing special—gray, slightly heart-shaped, the kind of thing you’d overlook. But sometimes I take it out on the train and rub my thumb across its surface like a worry bead. It reminds me that time is not linear. That boy is still skipping rocks inside me somewhere. The man who became disappointed in him is also still here. They argue sometimes. The boy usually wins because he still believes in momentum.

There’s a jazz record playing in the other room. Coltrane. The saxophone sounds like it’s apologizing for something enormous. Music is the only language that admits we’re all broken in the exact same way and that’s somehow beautiful. I read once that the spaces between notes are where God lives. I think that’s true. The silence after a heartbreak. The pause before someone says “I love you” back. The three seconds after the doctor says the word “malignant” before your brain starts translating it into a future.

I’ve been trying to get better at being a person. This involves, among other things: remembering to water the plants, not checking my phone during conversations, saying yes to invitations even when my instinct is to disappear into a book for three days. Progress is slow. Yesterday I only doom-scrolled for twenty minutes instead of forty. Small victories.

Sometimes I imagine all the versions of myself that didn’t make it to this moment. The one who took that job in Seattle. The one who said the cruel thing instead of swallowing it. The one who kept the baby. They’re not ghosts exactly. More like echoes that got lost in the hallway of choices. I try to be kind to them when they visit at 3 a.m. They did their best with the information they had.

The wind is still blowing. Marjorie has caught something and is wrapping it with the patience of someone who knows time is not the enemy. I should sleep. Instead I’m writing this because the page feels like the only honest friend I have at this hour. It doesn’t need me to be brilliant or healed or even particularly coherent. It just holds whatever I pour into it.

There’s a line from a poem I can’t remember properly: “We are all just walking each other home.” I like that. It suggests the journey is communal even when it feels solitary. That the wind rattling these windows is rattling someone else’s too. That somewhere right now another person is lying awake thinking about their own spider, their own stone, their own small failures that somehow add up to a life.

The radiator clanks again. Marjorie pauses her work. For one brief moment the whole apartment seems to be listening.

I whisper into the dark: “We’re doing okay, I think.”

The dark doesn’t answer, but it doesn’t disagree either.

That feels like enough for tonight.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a house I’ve never actually lived in but somehow remember perfectly. It’s 3:17 a.m. in the memory and the power is out. A candle the color of old teeth is burning on the kitchen table, throwing long crooked shadows that look like they’re arguing with each other. I’m sitting there barefoot, maybe eight years old, maybe thirty-eight, it’s hard to tell in candlelight. There’s a glass of warm milk in front of me that nobody asked for and a notebook with half the pages torn out. On the remaining ones I’ve written the same sentence seventeen times in different handwriting: “I promise I will not become the kind of adult who forgets this feeling.”

Outside, something large moves through the wet grass. Not an animal. More like the night itself stretching. I don’t look up. Some things are allowed to pass if you don’t give them names.

I remember suddenly that I’m not actually writing this from that kitchen. I’m in a different room, years later, typing on a machine that hums like it’s disappointed in me. My shoulders hurt. My coffee is cold. There’s a plant on the windowsill that’s been dead for so long it’s achieved a kind of dignity. I keep watering it anyway. We all need someone to pretend we’re still worth the effort.

The mind is a strange country with bad border control. Thoughts come in wearing someone else’s clothes and you let them stay because they seem familiar. Right now a memory of my grandmother is trying to cross. She’s making biscuits at 5 a.m. because she says dawn is the only time flour behaves itself. She lets me cut the shapes and I make them all into lopsided hearts because I’m six and in love with the concept of love. She doesn’t correct me. That’s the thing I keep coming back to. She never corrected the shape of my affection. Just dusted it with sugar and put it in the oven.

I wonder what she’d think of the person I became. Not in the big ways. In the small ones. The way I say “I’m fine” when I mean “I am a haunted house that learned how to pay taxes.” The way I apologize to furniture when I bump into it. The way I still can’t eat biscuits without feeling like I’m betraying some sacred geometry of childhood.

There’s a bird outside my window right now making a sound like it’s filing a complaint with God. I respect that energy. I’ve been trying to be more like that bird. Louder about my complaints. Less polite about my miracles. Yesterday I told a barista that her smile rearranged the atoms in the room and she looked at me like I’d escaped from somewhere. Maybe I have.

I keep thinking about how every person walking around is carrying an entire universe in their chest that no one else will ever fully visit. All those private summers. All those private apocalypses. The way someone can be crying in a supermarket aisle because the cereal brand changed its box and it reminds them of the year their dad left. We’re all just soft animals pretending to be competent at capitalism.

Sometimes I want to stop every stranger I pass and say: I see you. I see the way you’re trying. I see the small kindnesses you perform when you think no one’s watching. The way you let the person with three items go ahead of you even though you’re late. The way you talk to your houseplants in a slightly different voice than you use with humans. The way you keep choosing to stay even when staying feels like swallowing glass. I see it. I’m proud of you. Keep going.

But of course I don’t say it. I just nod like a normal person and continue pretending I’m not made of the same trembling stardust.

There are 1000 words here somewhere. I’m running out of them the way summer runs out of daylight. The candle in my mind is getting low. The rain has stopped. Whatever was moving through the grass has either left or become part of the landscape. Both possibilities feel equally true.

I think what I’m trying to say, in this messy sideways way, is that I’m still that kid at the table trying to write a promise in seventeen different handwritings. I still don’t want to become the kind of adult who forgets this feeling, whatever this feeling is. The one that makes you write 1000 words when someone says “write whatever comes to you.” The one that makes you love people you’ve never met because their playlists found you at 2 a.m. The one that makes you cry at commercials about dogs and grandfathers even though you’re a grown man who pays bills and has opinions about knives.

The feeling that says: stay soft. Stay ridiculous. Stay the kind of person who talks to birds and dead plants and the moon like they might answer back.

They do, sometimes.

If you listen like a child who hasn’t learned how not to.

The candle just went out.

I’m still here.
